free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg.t: An Alsatian wine town beneath a Hohenstaufen castle that was a free imperial city and Decapolis member until French annexation.
free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg.o: The castle of Kaysersberg was built in the 1220s for Frederick II to guard the route from Alsace into Lorraine over the Vosges, and a town grew at its foot. It received imperial-city privileges in 1293 and in 1354 joined the Decapolis, the defensive league of ten Alsatian imperial cities under the emperor's bailiff at Haguenau.
free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg.r: Ruled by a council and mayor, Kaysersberg was a modest community of vintners, craftsmen and traders whose wealth came from the wine of the surrounding slopes. The preacher Johann Geiler of Kaysersberg, the most famous pulpit voice of late medieval Strasbourg, grew up there and took his name from the town, which remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg.e: Like the other Decapolis cities it came under French protection after 1648, and the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679 completed its incorporation into the Kingdom of France. Albert Schweitzer was born there in 1875. It is now a small town in the Haut-Rhin department.

free-imperial-city-of-zell-am-harmersbac.t: One of the smallest free imperial cities, a Black Forest town in the Harmersbach valley that kept its independence until 1803.
free-imperial-city-of-zell-am-harmersbac.o: Zell grew in the Harmersbach valley near the abbey of Gengenbach and was recognised as a free imperial city in the 14th century, with its status confirmed in 1366. With the Free Imperial City of Gengenbach and Offenburg it lay within the Ortenau bailiwick, which emperors often pledged to neighbouring lords.
free-imperial-city-of-zell-am-harmersbac.r: With only a few hundred inhabitants, Zell was among the tiniest imperial estates, governed by a council and mayor. The town and the neighbouring free valley of Harmersbach, an unusual imperial community of peasants, lived from forestry, farming and crafts. Zell remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-zell-am-harmersbac.e: The mediatisation of 1803 gave Zell to Baden. Its pottery works, founded in 1794 and later known as Zeller Keramik, made the town's name in the 19th century. It is now a small town in Baden-Württemberg.

fort-dauphin-colony.t: France's first colony on Madagascar, a struggling trading post on the south-east coast that ended in massacre and evacuation in 1674.
fort-dauphin-colony.o: In 1643 the French Company of the East (Compagnie de l'Orient) sent Jacques Pronis to establish a post in south-east Madagascar. He founded Fort-Dauphin, named after the future Louis XIV, in the lands of the Antanosy Kingdom near modern Taolagnaro.
fort-dauphin-colony.r: The colony was small, poorly supplied and frequently mutinous, relying on cattle and rice obtained from the Antanosy by trade or raiding. Etienne de Flacourt, governor from 1648 to 1655, wrote a detailed history of Madagascar. Colonists also settled Bourbon (Reunion), and the post came under the new French East India Company in 1664.
fort-dauphin-colony.e: Mounting conflict with the Antanosy culminated in an attack in 1674, after which the surviving French evacuated to Bourbon and India. France later used the episode to justify its claims to Madagascar.

free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.t: Smallest north German republic of the Weimar era, the successor of the grand duchy, merged with its neighbour by the Nazis.
free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.o: Grand Duke Adolf Frederick VI died in February 1918 without a direct heir, leaving the throne in dispute. After the November revolution a state council took over, and Mecklenburg-Strelitz became a free state, adopting a constitution in 1919 and ending the archaic feudal constitution of 1755.
free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.r: The free state was a parliamentary republic with a Landtag elected by universal suffrage, governed from Neustrelitz. It remained rural, poor and sparsely populated, with large estates, and included the detached district of Ratzeburg. Its small size made it financially weak, and governments alternated between Social Democrats and conservative parties.
free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.e: After the Nazi seizure of power the Landtag was dissolved. On 1 January 1934 a Reich law merged it with the Free State of Mecklenburg-Schwerin into the Free State of Mecklenburg.

first-portuguese-republic.t: Portugal's first republic, an era of anticlerical reform and chronic instability with some 45 governments in under 16 years.
first-portuguese-republic.o: After the assassination of King Carlos I in 1908, republican sentiment grew in Lisbon. On 5 October 1910 a revolt by soldiers, sailors and Carbonária militants overthrew Manuel II, and a provisional government under Teófilo Braga proclaimed the republic, ending the Kingdom of Portugal.
first-portuguese-republic.r: The Constitution of 1911 created a parliamentary republic. Governments led by Afonso Costa separated Church and state, expelled the Jesuits and legalised divorce. Portugal entered the First World War in 1916 and suffered heavy losses at La Lys in 1918. Strikes, coups, bombings and Sidónio Pais's brief dictatorship of 1917-1918 marked the period, along with the royalist Monarchy of the North.
first-portuguese-republic.e: On 28 May 1926 a military coup led by General Gomes da Costa overthrew the republic and set up the Ditadura Nacional.

free-imperial-city-of-heilbronn.t: A Neckar wine and trading city whose imperial charter of 1371 made it a self-governing republic of burghers until 1802.
free-imperial-city-of-heilbronn.o: Heilbronn grew around a royal estate at a Neckar crossing, first mentioned in 741. The town received a charter from Rudolf I in 1281, and in 1371 Charles IV granted it a constitution that confirmed its status as a free imperial city and gave power to a council drawn from patricians and guildsmen.
free-imperial-city-of-heilbronn.r: Heilbronn lived from Neckar shipping, which it controlled through its weir, and from vineyards. The city accepted the Reformation in 1528 under the preacher Johann Lachmann. The knight Götz von Berlichingen was held prisoner in its tower in 1519, and in 1633 Sweden and the Protestant estates concluded the Heilbronn League there.
free-imperial-city-of-heilbronn.e: Heilbronn was annexed by Württemberg in 1802 and became part of the Kingdom of Württemberg in 1806. Heavily bombed in December 1944, it was rebuilt and is now an industrial and wine centre in Baden-Württemberg.

franks.t: A confederation of Germanic peoples on the lower Rhine whose kings conquered Gaul and founded the realm from which France and Germany both grew.
franks.o: The Franks ('the bold' or 'the free') appear in Roman sources around 250, a grouping of older Rhineland peoples such as the Chamavi, Chattuarii, Bructeri and Sugambri. They raided Gaul by land and sea, while many served as Roman soldiers. In 358 Julian allowed the Salian Franks to settle in Toxandria, in the modern Netherlands and Belgium.
franks.r: The confederation was led by many petty kings, with Salian Franks in the north-west and Rhineland Franks around Cologne. Franks rose high in Roman service, among them the generals Arbogast and Bauto. The grave of King Childeric I at Tournai, found in 1653, shows a ruler wearing both a Roman officer's cloak brooch and Frankish weapons.
franks.e: In 481 Childeric's son Clovis I became king and united the Frankish groups, defeating the Roman ruler Syagrius in 486 and converting to Catholic Christianity. His Merovingian kingdom, Francia, absorbed the Alemanni and Thuringians and passed later to the Carolingians, whose divisions produced East Francia and France.

free-imperial-city-of-aalen.t: A small imperial city at the edge of the Swabian Jura, built beside the largest Roman cavalry fort on the Raetian limes.
free-imperial-city-of-aalen.o: Aalen stands beside the largest Roman cavalry fort north of the Alps, built in the 2nd century on the Raetian limes. The medieval town was founded around 1240 under the Hohenstaufen. After a period pledged to the counts of Oettingen, it was recognised as a free imperial city by Charles IV in 1360.
free-imperial-city-of-aalen.r: One of the smallest imperial cities, Aalen was governed by a council and lived from crafts, farming, trade and iron ore mined nearby. It adopted the Reformation in 1575 and belonged to the Swabian Circle. A great fire in 1634, during the Thirty Years' War, destroyed much of the town.
free-imperial-city-of-aalen.e: In 1802 and 1803 Aalen was annexed by Württemberg, becoming part of the Kingdom of Württemberg in 1806. Today it is a city in Baden-Württemberg, and its Limes Museum stands on the site of the Roman fort.

french-second-republic.t: The short republic of 1848 that introduced universal male suffrage and abolished slavery, then elected the president who would overthrow it.
french-second-republic.o: The February Revolution of 1848 toppled the July Monarchy. A provisional government including the poet Alphonse de Lamartine proclaimed the Republic, introduced universal male suffrage, abolished slavery in the colonies under Victor Schoelcher's decree, and created National Workshops for the unemployed.
french-second-republic.r: The elected assembly was conservative, and the closure of the National Workshops provoked the June Days uprising, crushed by General Cavaignac with thousands killed. In December 1848 Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, nephew of Napoleon, was elected president by a landslide. The assembly then restricted suffrage and passed the Falloux law strengthening Church schools.
french-second-republic.e: Barred from a second term, Louis-Napoléon staged a coup on 2 December 1851, approved by plebiscite. A year later, on 2 December 1852, he proclaimed himself Emperor Napoleon III, founding the Second French Empire.

frisian-freedom.t: A medieval coastal society without lords, in which Frisian farmers governed themselves through elected judges and assemblies for nearly four centuries.
frisian-freedom.o: After the Carolingian counts lost effective control of the North Sea coast in the 11th and 12th centuries, the Frisian lands between the Vlie and the Weser governed themselves. Frisians claimed their liberty came from a privilege granted by Charlemagne, a legend that justified their refusal to accept feudal lords.
frisian-freedom.r: Each land or community chose its own judges, called redjeven or consuls, and delegates of the Seven Sealands met at the Upstalsboom near Aurich. Frisians built dykes and terps, raised cattle and traded by sea, and wrote down their own laws in Old Frisian. There were no knights or castles in the usual sense, but powerful chieftains, the hoofdelingen, rose in the 14th century.
frisian-freedom.e: Feuds between the Schieringers and Vetkopers weakened the Frisians in the 15th century. East Frisia came under the Cirksena counts in 1464, and in 1498 Emperor Maximilian made Albert of Saxony governor of Friesland, ending the freedom west of the Ems and creating the Lordship of Frisia.

free-state-of-fiume.t: Internationally recognised independent city-state around the port of Fiume, created to settle the dispute between Italy and Yugoslavia and annexed by Italy in 1924.
free-state-of-fiume.o: The Treaty of Rapallo, signed by Italy and the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in November 1920, created the Free State of Fiume as a compromise over the disputed port. After Italian forces ended D'Annunzio's Italian Regency of Carnaro in January 1921, elections in April 1921 were won by the Autonomist Party of Riccardo Zanella, who favoured independence.
free-state-of-fiume.r: Zanella's government struggled with economic collapse, as the port had lost its Hungarian hinterland, and with violent opposition from Italian nationalists and Fascists. In March 1922 a Fascist coup drove Zanella into exile, and Italian military authorities effectively took over. The population was mainly Italian, Croatian and Hungarian.
free-state-of-fiume.e: By the Treaty of Rome in January 1924, Italy and Yugoslavia partitioned the territory: Italy annexed Fiume, while Yugoslavia received the neighbouring Sušak district. After the Second World War the city became Rijeka in Yugoslavia, and most Italians left.

french-first-republic.t: The revolutionary republic that executed a king, fought most of Europe, passed through the Terror and the Directory, and ended in Napoleon's empire.
french-first-republic.o: After the storming of the Tuileries in August 1792, a newly elected National Convention abolished the monarchy of the Kingdom of France on 21 September 1792 and proclaimed the Republic. Louis XVI was tried and executed in January 1793, while French armies fought Austria, Prussia and Britain.
french-first-republic.r: Facing war and revolt, the Convention gave power to the Committee of Public Safety under Robespierre; the Terror executed thousands before his fall in July 1794. The Directory governed from 1795 amid corruption and coups. The Republic introduced the metric system, abolished feudal dues and slavery in 1794, and conquered Belgium, the Rhineland and Italy.
french-first-republic.e: Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in the coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799 and governed as First Consul, restoring order through the Concordat of 1801 and the Civil Code. In May 1804 the Republic was transformed into the First French Empire.

free-imperial-city-of-cologne.t: The largest city of medieval Germany, which broke free of its archbishops at Worringen in 1288 and stayed a Catholic imperial city until the French came in 1794.
free-imperial-city-of-cologne.o: Cologne grew from the Roman colony of Colonia Agrippina and was ruled for centuries by its archbishops. Its burghers fought them repeatedly, and the decisive victory came at the Battle of Worringen in 1288, after which the archbishops could no longer reside in the city. Emperor Frederick III formally confirmed its imperial status in 1475.
free-imperial-city-of-cologne.r: After 1396 the Verbundbrief gave political power to 22 guild-like associations. Cologne was the largest German city of the Middle Ages, a leading Hanseatic member trading wine, cloth and metalwork. Its citizens founded a university in 1388, and the cathedral, begun in 1248 to house the shrine of the Three Kings, drew pilgrims. Cologne remained firmly Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-cologne.e: French revolutionary troops occupied Cologne in 1794, and it was annexed to France. In 1815 it passed to Prussia and became the main city of the Rhine Province. The cathedral was completed in 1880 and is a World Heritage Site.

free-imperial-city-of-friedberg.t: Wetterau imperial city that shared its hill with a powerful imperial castle, whose knights gradually took control of the town.
free-imperial-city-of-friedberg.o: The Hohenstaufen emperors built a castle and founded a town at Friedberg on a ridge in the Wetterau, the town being documented as an imperial city in 1211. It lay on the trade route from Frankfurt to the north and held important fairs in the 13th century.
free-imperial-city-of-friedberg.r: The city council governed the burghers, but the castle's Burgraviate of Friedberg next door constantly competed with it. Friedberg joined the Wetterau city league with Frankfurt, Wetzlar and Gelnhausen. Cloth making and trade made it prosperous until the 14th century, and its Jewish community built a deep ritual bath around 1260 that survives. Debts and decline later left the town largely under the castle's influence.
free-imperial-city-of-friedberg.e: The city was pledged in 1455 and gradually dominated by the Burgraviate. It adopted Lutheranism and kept nominal imperial status until 1802, when it passed to Hesse-Darmstadt. It is now a town in Hesse.

francoist-spain.t: The dictatorship of Francisco Franco, born in the Spanish Civil War and lasting until his death in 1975.
francoist-spain.o: After the military coup of July 1936 against the Second Spanish Republic, the rebel generals named Francisco Franco head of state and Generalísimo at Burgos on 1 October 1936. Backed by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy, his Nationalists won the civil war in April 1939.
francoist-spain.r: Franco ruled through the army, the Church and a single party, FET y de las JONS, with harsh repression, executions and labour camps in the 1940s. Spain stayed out of the Second World War, apart from sending the Blue Division to Russia. Cold War alliance with the United States in 1953 ended isolation, and the Stabilisation Plan of 1959 brought rapid growth, tourism and urbanisation.
francoist-spain.e: In 1969 Franco named Juan Carlos de Borbón as his successor. ETA killed Prime Minister Luis Carrero Blanco in 1973. Franco died on 20 November 1975, and Juan Carlos became king, opening the transition to the democratic Kingdom of Spain.

free-county-of-burgundy.t: Franche-Comté, the imperial county of Burgundy across the Saône, rich in salt and fiercely loyal to its Habsburg rulers until Louis XIV conquered it.
free-county-of-burgundy.o: Otto-William, a grandson of Berengar of Italy, gathered the counties east of the Saône in the 980s and founded the comital house. The county lay in the Kingdom of Arles and so in the Holy Roman Empire, unlike the neighbouring Duchy of Burgundy, which was a French fief.
free-county-of-burgundy.r: Salt springs at Salins and Lons-le-Saunier provided the county's wealth, and a parliament sat at Dole. Countess Beatrice married Frederick Barbarossa in 1156, tying the county to the Hohenstaufen. Through marriage it passed to Philip the Bold in 1384 and joined the Burgundian State, then went with Mary of Burgundy to the Habsburgs and the Spanish crown.
free-county-of-burgundy.e: Louis XIV invaded in 1668 and again in 1674. The Treaty of Nijmegen in 1678 gave the county to the Kingdom of France, which moved its capital to Besançon. Its lasting name, Franche-Comté, recalls its separate past.

free-imperial-city-of-dinkelsbuhl.t: A walled imperial city on the Wörnitz whose intact medieval fortifications make it one of Germany's best-preserved old towns.
free-imperial-city-of-dinkelsbuhl.o: Dinkelsbühl grew at a crossing of trade routes on the Wörnitz and received town rights under the Hohenstaufen. After being pledged by the crown to various lords, it secured its status as a free imperial city in 1351, when Charles IV promised that it would not be pledged again.
free-imperial-city-of-dinkelsbuhl.r: In 1387 the guilds won a share of power in the council. Cloth, scythe-making and trade brought prosperity, visible in the late Gothic church of Saint George. The town became mixed in religion, and the Peace of Westphalia made it one of four imperial cities where Catholics and Lutherans shared council offices equally.
free-imperial-city-of-dinkelsbuhl.e: Swedish troops occupied the town in the Thirty Years' War, but it escaped destruction; local tradition says its children persuaded the Swedish colonel to spare it, a story celebrated in the Kinderzeche festival. In 1802 it passed to Bavaria. Its walls, gates and houses survive almost intact.

free-imperial-city-of-offenburg.t: Ortenau imperial city at the mouth of the Kinzig valley, often pledged to neighbours and burned by the French in 1689.
free-imperial-city-of-offenburg.o: Offenburg grew at the crossing of the Rhine valley road and the Kinzig valley into the Black Forest, under the dukes of Zähringen. After their line died out in 1218, it fell to the Hohenstaufen and by the 1240s was treated as an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-offenburg.r: The town was governed by a council and lived from its market, crafts and the Kinzig timber trade. With the rest of the Ortenau it was repeatedly pledged by the emperors to neighbouring lords, including the bishops of Strasbourg and the Palatinate, which limited its independence. After a brief Protestant phase it remained Catholic. French troops burned the town in 1689 during the Nine Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-offenburg.e: Offenburg lost its freedom in 1803 and was annexed by Baden. In 1847 the Offenburg Programme of the democratic movement was proclaimed there. It is now a town in Baden-Württemberg.

further-austria.t: The Habsburgs' scattered western lands in Swabia, Alsace and the Breisgau, governed for four centuries from Ensisheim and Freiburg.
further-austria.o: The Habsburgs came from the County of Habsburg in Aargau and held scattered lands across Swabia, Alsace and the upper Rhine. The Treaty of Neuberg of 1379 divided the family's possessions, giving the western territories, together with Tyrol and Inner Austria, to Leopold III; these western lands became known as Further Austria.
further-austria.r: Further Austria was a patchwork: the Breisgau with Freiburg, the Sundgau in Alsace, the forest towns on the Rhine, the margraviate of Burgau and the county of Hohenberg. It was governed from Ensisheim and later Freiburg, often together with the County of Tyrol, and had its own estates. Heavy losses to the Swiss followed in the 15th century. The University of Freiburg was founded in 1457.
further-austria.e: The Peace of Westphalia gave the Alsatian lands to France in 1648. After the Peace of Pressburg in 1805 the remaining territories were divided among the Grand Duchy of Baden, the Kingdom of Württemberg and the Kingdom of Bavaria, ending Habsburg rule in south-west Germany.

free-city-of-frankfurt.t: Self-governing city-republic on the Main that hosted the German Federal Diet and the 1848 Frankfurt Parliament.
free-city-of-frankfurt.o: Frankfurt, a free imperial city for centuries and the place of imperial elections and coronations, had been part of Dalberg's Grand Duchy of Frankfurt. The Congress of Vienna restored it in 1815 as one of four free cities of the German Confederation, and a constitution was adopted in 1816.
free-city-of-frankfurt.r: The city was governed by a senate and legislative assembly dominated by its wealthy Lutheran citizens. It was the seat of the Federal Diet and a major banking centre, home of the Rothschild bank. In 1848-49 the Frankfurt Parliament, the first freely elected German national assembly, met in St Paul's Church and drafted a constitution for a united Germany.
free-city-of-frankfurt.e: Frankfurt sided with Austria in 1866. Prussian troops occupied it, imposed a heavy indemnity, and the city was annexed to Prussia within the Province of Hesse-Nassau; its mayor, Karl Fellner, took his own life.

free-state-of-schaumburg-lippe.t: One of Germany's smallest republics, a successor of the Bückeburg principality that resisted absorption until 1946.
free-state-of-schaumburg-lippe.o: Prince Adolf II of Schaumburg-Lippe abdicated on 15 November 1918, and the principality became a free state, with a constitution adopted in 1922 and Bückeburg as capital.
free-state-of-schaumburg-lippe.r: With around 50,000 inhabitants, the state was largely rural, with sandstone quarrying and coal mining at Obernkirchen. Proposals to merge with Prussia failed in the 1920s, and the state kept its small parliament until the Nazis took power and placed it under a Reich governor shared with Lippe. Its tiny size made it a symbol of German particularism.
free-state-of-schaumburg-lippe.e: After 1945 it was in the British zone, and in November 1946 it was merged with Hanover, Brunswick and Oldenburg into Lower Saxony. The former princely family still lives at Bückeburg Palace, and the district of Schaumburg preserves the name.

french-mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.t: The League of Nations mandate under which France governed Syria and Lebanon between the world wars, shaping both modern states.
french-mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.o: The San Remo conference of April 1920 assigned Syria and Lebanon to France. French forces overthrew the Arab Kingdom of Syria at Maysalun that July, and the League of Nations formally confirmed the mandate in 1923.
french-mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.r: France ruled through a high commissioner in Beirut and divided the territory into Greater Lebanon, the states of Damascus and Aleppo, the Alawite State, the Jabal Druze State and the Sanjak of Alexandretta, often favouring minorities. The Great Syrian Revolt of 1925-1927, led by Sultan al-Atrash, was crushed after French artillery shelled Damascus. A 1936 treaty promising independence was never ratified by France, and in 1939 Alexandretta was ceded to Turkey.
french-mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.e: After British and Free French forces took the territories from Vichy France in 1941, independence was proclaimed. Lebanon gained real control in 1943, and the last French troops left Syria in April and Lebanon in December 1946.
french-mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.re: Sunni Islam, Christianity, Alawite and Druze communities

free-imperial-city-of-nuremberg.t: Franconian imperial city of Dürer and Hans Sachs, keeper of the imperial regalia and one of the great trading and craft centres of early modern Europe.
free-imperial-city-of-nuremberg.o: Nuremberg grew around an imperial castle first recorded in 1050 on a sandstone ridge above the Pegnitz. Its merchants gained privileges from the Salian and Hohenstaufen emperors, and in 1219 Frederick II's Great Charter of Freedom laid the basis for its self-government, gradually freeing it from the Hohenzollern burgraves who held the castle.
free-imperial-city-of-nuremberg.r: A closed circle of patrician families ran the council, excluding guilds from power. Metalwork, instruments, weapons and long-distance trade made the city rich, and from 1424 to 1796 it kept the imperial regalia. Albrecht Dürer, Veit Stoss, Hans Sachs and Martin Behaim, maker of the oldest surviving globe, worked there. Nuremberg turned Lutheran in 1525 and won a large rural territory in the Landshut War of 1504 to 1505.
free-imperial-city-of-nuremberg.e: War, debts and shifting trade routes weakened the city after 1600. In 1806 it was annexed by the Kingdom of Bavaria. It became a major industrial centre, and its old town was largely destroyed in 1945 and rebuilt.

free-imperial-city-of-obernai.t: Alsatian wine town below Mont Sainte-Odile, birthplace of Alsace's patron saint and a member of the Decapolis league of imperial cities.
free-imperial-city-of-obernai.o: Obernai lies at the foot of Mont Sainte-Odile and is held to be the birthplace of Saint Odile, patron saint of Alsace. A Hohenstaufen town, it was recognised as an imperial city in the 1280s, around 1283, and in 1354 it joined the Decapolis, the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities.
free-imperial-city-of-obernai.r: A council of burghers ruled this prosperous small town, which lived from wine, grain and crafts. Its market square, town hall and corn hall reflect late medieval and Renaissance prosperity. Obernai remained Catholic during the Reformation. Like the other Decapolis cities, it suffered heavily during the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-obernai.e: After the Peace of Westphalia gave France rights in Alsace, French troops occupied the Decapolis, and the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679 confirmed French rule. Obernai is now a town in Alsace, France.

free-state-of-waldeck.t: Small Hessian republic, successor of the Principality of Waldeck-Pyrmont, which gave up its independence in stages to Prussia.
free-state-of-waldeck.o: Prince Friedrich of Waldeck-Pyrmont was deposed in November 1918, and the principality became a free state with Arolsen as capital. Waldeck had been administered by Prussia under an accession treaty since 1868, so its independence was already limited.
free-state-of-waldeck.r: The free state was rural and poor, with farming and forestry in the hills around the Eder. Its finances depended on Prussian support. In 1921 the inhabitants of the detached district of Pyrmont voted to join Prussia, and Pyrmont passed to the Province of Hanover in 1922. The remaining state struggled to sustain its own government.
free-state-of-waldeck.e: After a treaty with Prussia, the Free State of Waldeck was absorbed into Prussia on 1 April 1929 and became part of the Province of Hesse-Nassau. It is now in the state of Hesse.

free-imperial-city-of-rosheim.t: The smallest of the Alsatian Decapolis cities, a wine town known for its Romanesque church of Saints Peter and Paul.
free-imperial-city-of-rosheim.o: Rosheim, at the foot of the Vosges west of Strasbourg, was an imperial possession under the Hohenstaufen. The town was walled in the 13th century and its rights as a free imperial city were confirmed around 1303. In 1354 it joined the Decapolis, the alliance of ten Alsatian imperial cities under the imperial bailiff at Haguenau.
free-imperial-city-of-rosheim.r: A council of burghers governed this small community of vintners, farmers and craftsmen. Its church of Saints Peter and Paul, built in the 12th century of yellow sandstone, is one of the finest Romanesque buildings in Alsace, and the town also preserves a stone house of the same age. Rosheim remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-rosheim.e: The town suffered heavily in the Thirty Years' War. After 1648 the Decapolis came under French protection, and the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1679 confirmed its incorporation into the Kingdom of France. It is now a small town in the Bas-Rhin department.

free-city-of-danzig-1807-1814.t: A Napoleonic city-state created at Tilsit, nominally free but in practice a French fortress on the Baltic.
free-city-of-danzig-1807-1814.o: After defeating Prussia, Napoleon created the Free City of Danzig by the Treaty of Tilsit in 1807, taking the city and its surrounding territory from the Kingdom of Prussia. It was placed under the joint protection of Prussia and the Kingdom of Saxony, whose king also ruled the Duchy of Warsaw.
free-city-of-danzig-1807-1814.r: The city had a senate and its own constitution, but real power lay with the French governor, General Jean Rapp, and a large garrison. Napoleon's Continental System cut off Danzig's trade with Britain and ruined its merchants, while the city had to pay heavy contributions. It served as a base for the 1812 invasion of Russia.
free-city-of-danzig-1807-1814.e: In 1813 Russian and Prussian forces besieged the city for most of the year, and Rapp surrendered at the end of 1813, the garrison leaving in January 1814. The Congress of Vienna returned Danzig to Prussia in 1815.

french-madagascar.t: Madagascar as a French colony, from the overthrow of the Merina monarchy to the autonomous Malagasy Republic of 1958.
french-madagascar.o: After the conquest of 1895 and the end of the French Protectorate of Madagascar, France annexed the island in 1896. In February 1897 the governor-general Joseph Gallieni abolished the Merina monarchy and exiled Queen Ranavalona III to Algeria, then put down the Menalamba rising and subdued the coastal peoples.
french-madagascar.r: Gallieni and his successors imposed a head tax and forced labour, promoted French over English schooling and broke the power of the Merina elite. Coffee, vanilla, cloves and rice were exported, and Nosy Be, Diego-Suarez and the Comoros were attached. In 1942 British forces took the island from Vichy France, and it passed to the Free French.
french-madagascar.e: The nationalist uprising of 1947 was crushed with tens of thousands of deaths. Madagascar became the autonomous Malagasy Republic in October 1958 and fully independent on 26 June 1960 under President Philibert Tsiranana.

former-shu.t: The kingdom founded in Sichuan by the soldier Wang Jian, a wealthy refuge for Tang scholars and poets in the turmoil after the Tang collapse.
former-shu.o: Wang Jian, a soldier from Henan who had served in the palace army, seized Chengdu in 891 and became military governor of the region. The Tang made him Prince of Shu in 903. When Zhu Wen deposed the Tang in 907, Wang Jian refused to recognise the Later Liang and proclaimed himself emperor.
former-shu.r: Protected by mountains, the fertile Sichuan basin escaped the wars of the north and prospered from rice, silk, salt and tea. Many Tang officials and literati took refuge at Chengdu, among them the poet Wei Zhuang, who served as chief minister. The Huajian anthology of song lyrics was compiled there in 940, after the dynasty, but reflects the court culture it fostered.
former-shu.e: Wang Jian's son Wang Yan, who succeeded in 918, was extravagant and neglected government. In 925 a Later Tang army marched in and met little resistance; Wang Yan surrendered and was killed with his family in 926 on the way to Luoyang. Sichuan soon became independent again as Later Shu.

frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.t: Merovingian kingdom of the Rhône and Saône valleys, built on the old Kingdom of the Burgundians and ruled from Chalon-sur-Saône.
frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.o: The Franks conquered the Kingdom of the Burgundians in 534. At the division of 561 Chlothar I's son Guntram received Burgundy with Orléans, ruling from Chalon-sur-Saône. The kingdom stretched from the Loire to the Alps and the Mediterranean.
frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.r: Guntram, a long-reigning king later venerated as a saint, acted as mediator between his feuding brothers' kingdoms. Burgundy kept its Roman law and Gallo-Roman aristocracy and its own mayor of the palace. The Irish monk Columbanus founded Luxeuil there, but was expelled by King Theuderic II and Brunhild.
frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.e: After 613 Burgundy was ruled together with Neustria by Chlothar II and his successors, though it kept a separate identity. It passed under Pippinid control, and Charles Martel subdued it in the 730s. With Pippin's accession in 751 it became a region of the Frankish realm.

free-state-bottleneck.t: Accidental mini-state in the Rhine valley, left unoccupied between French and American zones after the First World War.
free-state-bottleneck.o: The armistice of 1918 gave the Allies bridgeheads on the right bank of the Rhine, drawn as circles of 30 kilometres around Koblenz and Mainz. The two circles left a narrow gap near Lorch and Kaub, cut off from unoccupied Germany by hills, which became known from January 1919 as the Free State Bottleneck.
free-state-bottleneck.r: The area of some 17,000 people had no direct road or rail link with Germany. Lorch's mayor, Edmund Pnischeck, headed an improvised administration. Locals smuggled goods across the hills, printed their own emergency money and, in a famous episode, hijacked a French coal train to keep warm.
free-state-bottleneck.e: During the occupation of the Ruhr, French troops occupied the territory in February 1923, ending its separate existence. The area returned to German administration when the occupation ended in 1924.

free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-gmund.t: Swabian imperial city, perhaps the oldest Hohenstaufen town, home of the Parler family of master builders and long famous for gold and silver work.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-gmund.o: Gmünd is often called the oldest Hohenstaufen town, founded around 1162 near the family's ancestral castle on the Hohenstaufen hill. After the execution of Conradin, the last Hohenstaufen, in 1268, the town was not claimed by any prince and became an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-gmund.r: A council of patricians and later guilds governed the city. Heinrich Parler began the Holy Cross Minster there in the 14th century, one of the first German hall churches in the late Gothic style, and his son Peter Parler went on to build Prague Cathedral. Gold and silver smithing and the making of rosaries were its main trades. Gmünd remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-gmund.e: The city lost its freedom in 1802, when Württemberg annexed it. It remains a centre of the goldsmith's and silversmith's trade and is now a town in Baden-Württemberg, with the Holy Cross Minster at its heart.

free-imperial-city-of-lindau.t: Island city in Lake Constance, a trading gateway to Italy and Switzerland and one of four cities that signed the Tetrapolitan Confession in 1530.
free-imperial-city-of-lindau.o: Lindau grew around a convent of noble canonesses founded on an island in Lake Constance. The town became an important market and port, and after the Hohenstaufen era it gained recognition as an imperial city, around 1275, gradually limiting the convent's rights.
free-imperial-city-of-lindau.r: A council of patricians and guilds governed. Lindau thrived on trade over the lake and through the Alpine passes to Milan, served by the Lindau messenger service. The city hosted an imperial diet in 1496. It accepted the Reformation and in 1530 joined Strasbourg, Constance and Memmingen in presenting the Tetrapolitan Confession, later adopting Lutheranism.
free-imperial-city-of-lindau.e: In 1802 Lindau went to Prince Bretzenheim, then to Austria in 1804 and to Bavaria in 1805. It remains Bavarian, Bavaria's only town on Lake Constance, linked to the mainland by bridge and railway causeway.

free-imperial-city-of-augsburg.t: Swabian imperial city of the Fugger and Welser bankers, where the Augsburg Confession was read in 1530 and the Peace of Augsburg made in 1555.
free-imperial-city-of-augsburg.o: Augsburg grew from the Roman provincial capital of Augusta Vindelicorum and was ruled for centuries by its bishops. Its citizens won increasing self-government, and in 1276 King Rudolf I confirmed their town law, making Augsburg an imperial city independent of the Prince-Bishopric of Augsburg.
free-imperial-city-of-augsburg.r: A council of patricians and guilds governed after the guild revolution of 1368. Textile production and banking made Augsburg one of Europe's richest cities; the Fuggers financed emperors and founded the Fuggerei social housing in 1516. The Augsburg Confession was presented at the diet of 1530, and the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 recognised Lutheranism. After 1648 Catholics and Protestants shared offices equally.
free-imperial-city-of-augsburg.e: Augsburg lost its freedom in 1806 when it was annexed by the Kingdom of Bavaria. It remains a major Bavarian city, and the Peace Festival of 8 August, held since 1650, is still a local holiday.

free-state-of-saxony.t: Republican Saxony between the monarchy and East German centralisation, an industrial state of left-wing politics and later Soviet rule.
free-state-of-saxony.o: King Frederick Augustus III abdicated in November 1918, and workers' and soldiers' councils briefly took power. A Landtag was elected in 1919, and in 1920 a constitution established Saxony as a free state within the Weimar Republic, with Dresden as capital.
free-state-of-saxony.r: Saxony's industry made it a stronghold of the Social Democrats and Communists. In 1923 the government of Erich Zeigner, including Communists, was deposed by the federal government with troops. The Nazis took control in 1933, with Martin Mutschmann as Reich governor. Dresden was devastated by Allied bombing in February 1945, and Saxony fell in the Soviet occupation zone.
free-state-of-saxony.e: After 1945 Saxony was restored as a Land in the Soviet zone and in 1949 in the German Democratic Republic. In 1952 the GDR abolished the Länder, dividing Saxony into the districts of Dresden, Leipzig and Karl-Marx-Stadt; it was re-established in 1990.

free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen.t: Lake Constance imperial city whose grain market fed the region and whose walls held off Swedish sieges in the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen.o: Überlingen was a royal estate and Hohenstaufen town on the north shore of Lake Constance, with a harbour serving the grain trade across the lake. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen around 1268, it became an imperial city, confirmed by later kings, with a small territory of nearby villages.
free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen.r: A council dominated by guilds ruled. Its grain market supplied Switzerland and the lake region, and wine was another source of wealth. The town remained Catholic and loyal to the Habsburgs, and in 1632 and 1634 it withstood Swedish sieges. Its large Gothic minster of St. Nicholas holds a famous carved high altar by Jörg Zürn.
free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen.e: Überlingen lost its freedom in 1803 when it was annexed by Baden. In the 19th century its mineral spring made it a spa and resort town, and it is now in Baden-Württemberg, its minster and walls well preserved.

four-macedonian-republics.t: The four self-governing districts into which Rome split the old kingdom of Macedon after Pydna, a short-lived experiment that ended in revolt and annexation.
four-macedonian-republics.o: After defeating Perseus at Pydna in 168 BCE, Rome abolished the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia. In 167 BCE Lucius Aemilius Paullus announced the settlement at Amphipolis: Macedon was to be 'free' but divided into four republics (merides) with capitals at Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia.
four-macedonian-republics.r: Each republic had elected magistrates and a council, but contact between them was restricted: citizens could not marry or own land across the borders. The Macedonians paid Rome half the taxes they had paid their kings, the royal gold and silver mines were closed until 158 BCE and timber from the royal forests was banned. The first meris struck silver coins showing Artemis.
four-macedonian-republics.e: Resentment and disorder grew. In 149 BCE Andriscus, claiming to be a son of Perseus, reunited Macedon briefly as king. Quintus Caecilius Metellus defeated him in 148 BCE, and Macedonia became a Roman province in 146 BCE, with the Via Egnatia later binding it together.

falerii.t: Chief city of the Faliscans, a people who spoke a language close to Latin but lived within Etruscan culture, destroyed by Rome in 241 BCE.
falerii.o: Falerii, later called Falerii Veteres, stood on a steep tufa plateau at modern Civita Castellana in the Ager Faliscus, between the Tiber and Monte Cimino. It developed from Iron Age settlements of the 9th and 8th centuries BCE. The Faliscans spoke Faliscan, an Italic language closely related to Latin, though their art, cults and politics were tied to Etruria.
falerii.r: Falerii was famous for the cult of Juno Curitis, whose festival Ovid described, and for its temples decorated with fine terracottas. Its workshops produced Faliscan red-figure vases in the 4th century BCE. The city usually allied with Veii against Rome; Roman legend tells how Camillus, besieging it in 394 BCE, sent back a schoolmaster who tried to hand over his pupils, and the Faliscans surrendered in admiration.
falerii.e: After further wars Falerii revolted in 241 BCE, just after the First Punic War, and was crushed within days. Rome destroyed the hilltop city and moved its people to Falerii Novi on open ground about 6 km away, whose walls still stand. The old site was resettled in the Middle Ages as Civita Castellana.

free-state-of-icaria.t: Tiny independent republic declared on the Aegean island of Icaria in 1912 after islanders expelled the Ottoman garrison, lasting months until union with Greece.
free-state-of-icaria.o: Icaria, a mountainous island west of Samos, was under Ottoman rule when Italy's war with the Ottoman Empire weakened Turkish control in the Aegean. On 17 July 1912 the islanders, led by the doctor Ioannis Malachias, rose against the small Ottoman garrison, forced its surrender and proclaimed the Free State of Icaria.
free-state-of-icaria.r: The new state set up a provisional government at Agios Kirykos, adopted its own flag and issued postage stamps. It lacked money, an army and any outside recognition, and the islanders, who lived by farming, herding and emigration, hoped for annexation by Greece rather than lasting independence.
free-state-of-icaria.e: When the First Balkan War began, the Greek navy arrived in November 1912 and the island joined the Kingdom of Greece. The episode lasted about five months and is still commemorated on Icaria every July.

free-peoples-state-of-wurttemberg.t: Democratic successor of the Kingdom of Württemberg, a well-governed Weimar state that was split by the occupying powers in 1945.
free-peoples-state-of-wurttemberg.o: In November 1918 King William II abdicated, and a provisional government of Social Democrats and Independents declared a republic in Stuttgart. A constitution adopted in 1919 created the Free People's State of Württemberg.
free-peoples-state-of-wurttemberg.r: Württemberg had a balanced economy of small farms and skilled industry, with companies such as Bosch and Daimler. Governments were led by the Centre and conservatives, including Eugen Bolz from 1928, who was later executed for his part in the resistance to Hitler. After 1933 the Nazi Reich governor Wilhelm Murr ruled the state.
free-peoples-state-of-wurttemberg.e: After 1945 the state was divided by the occupying powers: the northern part, in the American zone, joined northern Baden as Württemberg-Baden, and the southern part, under the French, became Württemberg-Hohenzollern. They merged into Baden-Württemberg in 1952.

funj-sultanate.t: The Sultanate of Sennar, which replaced Christian Alodia and ruled the middle Nile for three centuries, spreading Islam across Sudan.
funj-sultanate.o: In 1504 the Funj leader Amara Dunqas founded Sennar on the Blue Nile. Allied with the Arab chief Abdallah Jamma of the Abdallab Sheikhdom, the Funj destroyed Alodia and its capital Soba, establishing a sultanate that dominated the Gezira and the Nile valley north to the third cataract.
funj-sultanate.r: The sultan ruled through vassal lords, among them the Abdallab, who held the north. Sennar grew rich on gold, slaves and caravan trade with Egypt and the Red Sea. Sufi teachers and Islamic schools spread Islam and Arabic among the population. Badi II created a slave army, and later sultans were dominated by the Hamaj regents from 1761.
funj-sultanate.e: Weakened by civil wars, Sennar fell to Ismail Pasha's army in 1821 as Egypt under Muhammad Ali conquered Sudan, creating the Turco-Egyptian Sudan. The last sultan, Badi VII, submitted without a fight.

free-state-of-anhalt.t: Small central German republic that hosted the Bauhaus at Dessau and in 1932 became the first state with a Nazi head of government.
free-state-of-anhalt.o: Duke Joachim Ernst's regent abdicated in November 1918, and the Duchy of Anhalt became a free state, with a democratic constitution adopted in 1919 and Dessau as capital.
free-state-of-anhalt.r: Anhalt was governed by Social Democratic coalitions for most of the 1920s. Its industries included the Junkers aircraft works and chemical plants at Bitterfeld nearby. In 1925 the Bauhaus moved from Weimar to Dessau, where Walter Gropius designed its new building. After the Nazis won the 1932 state election, Alfred Freyberg became the first Nazi minister-president of a German state, and the Bauhaus was forced out that year.
free-state-of-anhalt.e: The Nazis subordinated Anhalt to a Reich governor. In 1945 it was occupied and placed in the Soviet zone, where it was merged with the Prussian Province of Saxony to form the province, later Land, of Saxony-Anhalt.

free-imperial-city-of-leutkirch.t: A small Allgäu linen town that remained a free imperial city for five centuries, until the German mediatisation of 1802.
free-imperial-city-of-leutkirch.o: Leutkirch grew up as the market centre of the Nibelgau in upper Swabia. In 1293 it received the town law of Lindau from King Adolf of Nassau, and it came to rank as a free imperial city answerable only to the emperor, although the imperial bailiwick over the surrounding countryside was often pledged to neighbouring lords.
free-imperial-city-of-leutkirch.r: A small council-governed town, Leutkirch lived from weaving linen and from the market of the surrounding farms. It adopted the Reformation in the 1540s, and its Protestant burghers coexisted uneasily with Catholic neighbours such as the local abbeys and the County of Waldburg. It sat in the Swabian Circle and on the Swabian bench of cities at the Imperial Diet.
free-imperial-city-of-leutkirch.e: The town suffered repeatedly in the Thirty Years' War. In 1802, as the mediatisation of the imperial cities began, Bavaria occupied it, and in 1810 it passed to the Kingdom of Württemberg. Today it is Leutkirch im Allgäu in Baden-Württemberg.

free-imperial-city-of-buchhorn.t: Tiny imperial city on the north shore of Lake Constance that was merged with a neighbouring priory to form the town of Friedrichshafen in 1811.
free-imperial-city-of-buchhorn.o: Buchhorn grew on the north shore of Lake Constance as a fishing and market settlement under the counts of Buchhorn and later the Guelphs and Hohenstaufen. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen it was recognised as an imperial city by Rudolf I around 1275.
free-imperial-city-of-buchhorn.r: Buchhorn was one of the smallest imperial cities, with a council of burghers and a tiny territory. It lived from fishing, lake shipping and trade across the lake to Switzerland, and its market served the surrounding countryside. It remained Catholic and depended on alliances with other Swabian cities and on Austrian goodwill.
free-imperial-city-of-buchhorn.e: Bavaria annexed Buchhorn in 1802 and passed it to Württemberg in 1810. In 1811 King Frederick I of Württemberg merged it with the neighbouring Hofen priory to create Friedrichshafen, later the home of the Zeppelin airships.

fib.t: A Pictish province between the Tay and the Forth, the ancestor of the Kingdom of Fife, named in the legend of the seven sons of Cruithne.
fib.o: Fib appears among the seven Pictish provinces named after the legendary sons of Cruithne. Its territory corresponded broadly to modern Fife and Kinross, between the Firth of Tay and the Firth of Forth.
fib.r: Nothing is known of its rulers in the Pictish period. The peninsula was fertile, and St Andrews, known earlier as Cennrigmonaid, became one of the leading Pictish churches, receiving relics of Saint Andrew by tradition in the 8th century.
fib.e: Fib became the earldom of Fife within the Kingdom of Scotland, whose earls held the right to enthrone the king at Scone. Fife still calls itself 'the Kingdom'.

free-imperial-city-of-rottweil.t: Swabian imperial city on Roman foundations, seat of an imperial court and for over a century an ally of the Swiss Confederacy.
free-imperial-city-of-rottweil.o: Rottweil grew on the site of the Roman town of Arae Flaviae on the upper Neckar. A royal estate in the Carolingian period, it was refounded by the Zähringen and Hohenstaufen and became an imperial city after their fall, by around 1268.
free-imperial-city-of-rottweil.r: The city was home to the Imperial Court of Rottweil, which heard cases from across south-western Germany. A council with strong guild participation governed it, and it acquired one of the largest territories of any Swabian imperial city. In 1519 it concluded a perpetual alliance with the Old Swiss Confederacy, as an associate member. It remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-rottweil.e: Rottweil lost its freedom in 1802 when Württemberg annexed it, and the imperial court was abolished. Its Swabian-Alemannic carnival, the Fasnet, remains famous, and it is now a town in Baden-Württemberg.

first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman.t: The first Ibadi state in Oman, an elected imamate centred on Nizwa that set the pattern for Omani religious government for a thousand years.
first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman.o: In 751 the Omani Ibadis elected al-Julanda ibn Mas'ud as their first imam, but he was killed the next year by an army of the new Abbasid Caliphate. After decades under local chiefs, the imamate was restored in 793 with the election of Muhammad ibn Affan, followed by Warith ibn Ka'b, and lasted a century.
first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman.r: Imams were chosen by the learned and leading men and could be deposed if they broke the law, an ideal of accountable leadership central to Ibadism. Nizwa became the capital and a centre of scholarship. Oman controlled the sea trade of the Gulf through Sohar, while the falaj irrigation channels supported date farming in the interior. al-Salt ibn Malik ruled for over thirty years.
first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman.e: The deposition of al-Salt ibn Malik in 886 split Omani scholars into rival schools and led to civil war. In 893 the Abbasid governor of Bahrain, Muhammad ibn Nur, invaded, sacked Nizwa and ended the imamate, though Ibadi imams reappeared repeatedly later.

finnish-socialist-workers-republic.t: Red Finland, the revolutionary government that held southern Finland during the civil war of 1918 before its defeat by the Whites and Germany.
finnish-socialist-workers-republic.o: Tensions after independence erupted into civil war in January 1918. On 28 January the Red Guards seized Helsinki, and the Finnish People's Delegation, chaired by Kullervo Manner, took power in the industrial south. In late February it was proclaimed the Finnish Socialist Workers' Republic.
finnish-socialist-workers-republic.r: The Reds controlled the cities and industrial centres of southern Finland, including Helsinki, Tampere, Turku and Viipuri. Their draft constitution mixed socialist ideas with parliamentary democracy, and they received arms from Soviet Russia. Both sides committed terror, and the Red administration struggled with food shortages and military weakness.
finnish-socialist-workers-republic.e: The White army under Mannerheim won the decisive Battle of Tampere in April 1918, while German troops took Helsinki. Red Finland collapsed in May, and about 80,000 Reds were held in prison camps, where some 12,000 died. Its leaders fled to Soviet Russia and founded the Communist Party of Finland.

free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg.t: A northern Alsatian imperial city that grew around a powerful Benedictine abbey and joined the Decapolis before passing to France.
free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg.o: Wissembourg grew around the Benedictine abbey of Saints Peter and Paul, founded in the 7th century on the Lauter, where the monk Otfrid wrote his Old High German Gospel Harmony in the 9th century. The townspeople slowly freed themselves from the abbot's lordship, and by the early 14th century the town ranked as a free imperial city. In 1354 it was a founding member of the Decapolis.
free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg.r: A council of burghers and guilds governed the town, which lived from wine, crafts and the road between Strasbourg and the Palatinate. The abbey remained a rival authority; it became a provostry in 1524 and was united with the Prince-Bishopric of Speyer in 1546. The Reformation won a following among the townspeople, while the abbey stayed Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg.e: Repeatedly fought over in the 17th century, Wissembourg came under French protection after 1648, and annexation by the Kingdom of France was confirmed by the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679. The exiled Polish king Stanisław Leszczyński later lived there. It is now a town in the Bas-Rhin department.

free-state-of-prussia.t: Republican Prussia, Germany's largest state and a democratic bulwark under Social Democrats until a coup in 1932.
free-state-of-prussia.o: With William II's abdication in November 1918 the Kingdom of Prussia became a republic. A constitution of 1920 created the Free State of Prussia, covering about three-fifths of Germany's territory and population, from East Prussia to the Rhineland, though it lost territory to Poland, Belgium and Denmark under the Treaty of Versailles.
free-state-of-prussia.r: Prussia was governed for most of the 1920s by a coalition of Social Democrats, the Catholic Centre and liberals under Minister-President Otto Braun, with a police force loyal to the republic. In July 1932 Chancellor Franz von Papen removed the Prussian government by decree, the Preußenschlag. Under the Nazis, Hermann Göring became minister-president and Prussia lost its separate statehood in practice.
free-state-of-prussia.e: After 1945 Prussia's eastern territories passed to Poland and the Soviet Union, and its Germans were expelled. The Allied Control Council formally abolished Prussia by Law No. 46 on 25 February 1947.

free-imperial-city-of-reutlingen.t: Swabian imperial city below the Jura that beat the Count of Württemberg in 1377 and was one of two cities to sign the Augsburg Confession in 1530.
free-imperial-city-of-reutlingen.o: Reutlingen grew at the foot of the Achalm hill on the edge of the Swabian Jura, and was fortified and granted town rights by the Hohenstaufen around 1240, becoming an imperial city. Its walls soon had to resist the counts of Württemberg, whose territory surrounded it.
free-imperial-city-of-reutlingen.r: Guilds came to dominate the council, an unusual feature among Swabian cities. In 1377 the townsmen defeated Ulrich of Württemberg at the Battle of Reutlingen, a high point of the Swabian city leagues. Cloth and leather were its main trades. Under the preacher Matthäus Alber it adopted the Reformation in the 1520s, and in 1530 it was one of only two cities to sign the Augsburg Confession, with Nuremberg.
free-imperial-city-of-reutlingen.e: A great fire in 1726 destroyed much of the town. Reutlingen lost its freedom in 1802, when it was annexed by Württemberg, and it is now a city in Baden-Württemberg; the Gothic Marienkirche survived the fire.

fidenae.t: Small town on the Tiber just north of Rome, allied with Veii, which Rome fought for repeatedly and finally destroyed in 426 BCE.
fidenae.o: Fidenae stood on a hill above the left bank of the Tiber, about 8 km north of Rome, opposite the Etruscan city of Veii. It was a Latin town, though Livy says it had Etruscan connections, and settlement there goes back to the early Iron Age. Its position on the river and the Via Salaria made it strategically vital.
fidenae.r: Little is known of its government. Roman tradition tells of repeated wars from the time of Romulus, as Fidenae shifted between Rome and Veii. In 438 BCE it went over to Lars Tolumnius of Veii and killed Roman envoys; the Roman officer Aulus Cornelius Cossus killed Tolumnius in single combat and dedicated his armour as the spolia opima.
fidenae.e: In 426 BCE the dictator Mamercus Aemilius captured and destroyed Fidenae, and its land became Roman. It survived only as a village; under Tiberius, in 27 CE, the collapse of a wooden amphitheatre there reportedly killed thousands, as Tacitus records.

free-imperial-city-of-regensburg.t: Danube city of Roman origin, a great medieval trading hub and from 1663 the permanent seat of the Imperial Diet of the Holy Roman Empire.
free-imperial-city-of-regensburg.o: Regensburg grew from the Roman legionary fortress of Castra Regina and became the seat of the Bavarian dukes and a bishop. Its merchants traded from Venice to Kiev, and the Stone Bridge over the Danube was built in the 1130s and 1140s. In 1245 Frederick II granted the city self-government, making it an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-regensburg.r: Patrician merchant families, whose tower houses still stand, ruled through the council. The bishop, several imperial abbeys and the city shared the town. Trade declined in the 15th century, and Regensburg briefly submitted to Bavaria from 1486 to 1492. It adopted Lutheranism in 1542. From 1663 to 1806 it hosted the Perpetual Imperial Diet, the Empire's standing assembly.
free-imperial-city-of-regensburg.e: In 1803 the city became part of the Principality of Regensburg under Karl Theodor von Dalberg, and in 1810 it passed to the Kingdom of Bavaria. Its medieval old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

free-imperial-city-of-speyer.t: A Rhineland cathedral city that hosted imperial diets and the Imperial Chamber Court and gave Protestantism its name in 1529.
free-imperial-city-of-speyer.o: Speyer, the Roman Noviomagus, was the burial place of the Salian emperors, whose cathedral rose there from 1030. The burghers gradually wrested power from the bishop, helped by Henry V's charter of 1111, and in 1294 the bishop gave up most of his remaining rights, leaving the city self-governing under the emperor alone.
free-imperial-city-of-speyer.r: Patricians and later the guilds shared power in the council. The city hosted some fifty imperial diets; at the 1529 diet the Lutheran estates issued the 'protestation' that gave Protestants their name. From 1527 to 1689 the Imperial Chamber Court, the empire's highest court, sat in Speyer. The city turned Lutheran, while the Prince-Bishopric of Speyer kept the cathedral Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-speyer.e: In 1689 French troops burned Speyer during the Nine Years' War, and the court moved to Wetzlar. Revolutionary France occupied the city in 1792 and annexed it in 1797. After 1816 it was the capital of the Bavarian Palatinate, and it now lies in Rhineland-Palatinate.

free-state-of-mecklenburg.t: Mecklenburg reunited by the Nazis in 1934, which after 1945 became a Land of the Soviet zone and the GDR until its abolition in 1952.
free-state-of-mecklenburg.o: On 1 January 1934 a Reich law merged the Free State of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and the Free State of Mecklenburg-Strelitz into a single Land of Mecklenburg, with Schwerin as capital, ending the division that dated from 1701.
free-state-of-mecklenburg.r: Under the Nazis the state was run by Reich governor Friedrich Hildebrandt. Rostock's Heinkel and Arado aircraft works made it a target of Allied bombing. In 1945 it was occupied by Soviet and British forces and placed in the Soviet zone, gaining western Pomerania and receiving many expellees. A land reform in 1945 broke up the large estates.
free-state-of-mecklenburg.e: Known as Mecklenburg-Vorpommern until 1947, the Land became part of the German Democratic Republic in 1949. In 1952 it was divided into the districts of Rostock, Schwerin and Neubrandenburg; the state was re-established in 1990 as Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

federal-republic-of-germany.t: Post-war German democracy, founded in the western zones in 1949 and enlarged by reunification in 1990.
federal-republic-of-germany.o: The three western occupation zones were combined, and a parliamentary council drafted the Basic Law, which came into force on 23 May 1949. Konrad Adenauer became the first chancellor, with Bonn as provisional capital, while the Soviet zone became the German Democratic Republic.
federal-republic-of-germany.r: Under the social market economy of Ludwig Erhard, West Germany experienced the Wirtschaftswunder. It joined NATO in 1955 and was a founding member of the European Economic Community in 1957. Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik eased relations with the East. The federal system gives strong powers to the Länder, and a Constitutional Court guards the Basic Law.
federal-republic-of-germany.e: After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the GDR joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990 under Helmut Kohl. Berlin became the capital, and Germany is today the European Union's most populous member and largest economy.

french-protectorate-of-madagascar.t: The French protectorate imposed on the Merina monarchy of Madagascar, a step between independence and outright colonial conquest.
french-protectorate-of-madagascar.o: France fought the Merina Kingdom in the Franco-Hova War of 1883-1885. The treaty of December 1885 gave France control over Madagascar's foreign relations, the bay of Diego-Suarez and a resident-general at Antananarivo, though the Merina government kept internal power.
french-protectorate-of-madagascar.r: Queen Ranavalona III and her prime minister and husband Rainilaiarivony continued to govern through a modernised administration, a Protestant state church and an army. They disputed French claims to a full protectorate, and Britain recognised French rights only in 1890. Debts from the war indemnity weakened the monarchy.
french-protectorate-of-madagascar.e: In 1895 a French expedition marched on Antananarivo, which fell in September. The Menalamba rising followed, and France annexed the island in 1896. In February 1897 General Gallieni abolished the monarchy and exiled the queen, making the island the colony of French Madagascar.

free-imperial-city-of-frankfurt.t: Main river trading city where German kings were elected and later crowned, famous for its fairs, its Jewish quarter and as birthplace of Goethe.
free-imperial-city-of-frankfurt.o: Frankfurt grew around a Carolingian palace at a ford over the Main. Royal assemblies met there, and its fairs grew into some of the most important in Europe. The citizens gained self-government in the 13th century, and from about 1245 it was treated as an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-frankfurt.r: A patrician council ruled. The Golden Bull of 1356 made Frankfurt the place of royal elections, and from 1562 coronations also took place in its cathedral. Its autumn fair and book fair drew merchants from across Europe. Jews lived in the walled Judengasse, attacked in the Fettmilch Uprising of 1614. The city turned Lutheran, and Goethe was born there in 1749.
free-imperial-city-of-frankfurt.e: In 1806 Frankfurt lost its freedom to Dalberg, becoming capital of the Grand Duchy of Frankfurt. In 1815 it became a free city, seat of the German Confederation and of the 1848 Frankfurt Parliament. Prussia annexed it in 1866.

free-and-independent-state-of-cundinamar.t: A centralist republic around Bogotá that fought rival federalists during Colombia's 'Foolish Fatherland' before the Spanish reconquest.
free-and-independent-state-of-cundinamar.o: After the Bogotá revolution of 20 July 1810, the province of Santa Fe proclaimed the State of Cundinamarca. Its constitution of 1811, under President Jorge Tadeo Lozano, still recognised Ferdinand VII as king. Antonio Nariño, who had translated the Rights of Man in 1794, soon took power and favoured a strong central government.
free-and-independent-state-of-cundinamar.r: Cundinamarca refused to join the federalist United Provinces of New Granada, and the two sides fought a civil war in 1812 and 1813. Nariño repelled a federalist attack on Bogotá in January 1813, and in July Cundinamarca declared full independence from Spain. Nariño then led a campaign against royalists in the south but was captured at Pasto in 1814.
free-and-independent-state-of-cundinamar.e: In December 1814 Simón Bolívar, serving the United Provinces, captured Bogotá and forced Cundinamarca to join the federation. Pablo Morillo's royalist army retook Bogotá in 1816, ending the first period of independence.

free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen.t: Town on the Kinzig founded by Frederick Barbarossa, whose imperial palace hosted the 1180 diet that stripped Henry the Lion of his duchies.
free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen.o: Emperor Frederick Barbarossa founded Gelnhausen in 1170 as a market town, granting it privileges and building an imperial palace on an island in the Kinzig river. It lay on the trade road from Frankfurt to Leipzig. In 1180 the palace hosted the imperial diet that issued the Gelnhausen Charter, dividing the lands of Henry the Lion.
free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen.r: As an imperial city Gelnhausen was governed by a council of burghers under the emperor's protection, prospering from trade along the road between Frankfurt and the east. Its Marienkirche, with an unusual eastern tower group, and the ruined palace are among the finest Hohenstaufen buildings. The town was too small to defend its autonomy for long once Hohenstaufen power collapsed.
free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen.e: In 1349 Emperor Charles IV pledged the city, and it passed to the Counts of Hanau and the Electoral Palatinate, which ruled it jointly. It kept a nominal imperial status until 1803, when it went to Hesse-Kassel. It is now a town in Hesse.

free-imperial-city-of-schweinfurt.t: Imperial city on the Main destroyed in the margrave war of 1554 and birthplace of the Leopoldina, Germany's oldest academy of sciences.
free-imperial-city-of-schweinfurt.o: Schweinfurt grew around a crossing of the Main and was rebuilt after destruction in the 13th century, being recognised as an imperial city around 1254. It lay between the lands of the bishops of Würzburg and the Hohenzollerns and had to defend its freedom against both.
free-imperial-city-of-schweinfurt.r: A council of burghers ruled, and the town lived from trade on the Main, crafts and wine. It adopted the Reformation in 1542. In the Second Margrave War Margrave Albert Alcibiades of Brandenburg-Kulmbach occupied it, and in 1554 his enemies destroyed the city. In 1652 four Schweinfurt physicians founded the academy later known as the Leopoldina.
free-imperial-city-of-schweinfurt.e: Schweinfurt lost its freedom in 1802 when Bavaria annexed it. In the 19th century it became an industrial town known for ball bearings, and it is now in Bavaria. The Leopoldina is Germany's national academy of sciences.

french-guiana.t: France's territory on the South American mainland, once a notorious penal colony and today home to Europe's spaceport at Kourou.
french-guiana.o: French attempts to settle Cayenne began in the early 17th century, including one in 1643 that ended in disaster. In 1664 a lasting settlement was established at Cayenne under Antoine Lefebvre de La Barre. The Dutch and English contested it, but France held it from 1676, apart from a Portuguese-Brazilian occupation from 1809 to 1817.
french-guiana.r: The colony produced sugar, spices and annatto with enslaved African labour, but the population remained small. The Kourou expedition of 1763 sent some 12,000 settlers, most of whom died of disease. Slavery was abolished in 1794, restored in 1802 and finally ended in 1848. From 1852 to 1953 the colony held a penal colony, the bagne, including the Îles du Salut, where Alfred Dreyfus was held on Devil's Island. Gold rushes drew prospectors from the 1850s.
french-guiana.e: French Guiana became an overseas department of France in 1946. The Guiana Space Centre opened at Kourou in 1968 and now launches European Ariane rockets. Since 2015 it has been a single territorial collectivity, part of the European Union.

free-imperial-city-of-kempten.t: Protestant imperial city that stood beside the Catholic Prince-Abbey of Kempten, two rival states sharing one town until 1803.
free-imperial-city-of-kempten.o: The town of Kempten grew beside the Prince-Abbey of Kempten, which originally held lordship over it. The burghers gained growing autonomy, and in 1289 King Rudolf I granted them the rights of an imperial city. Disputes with the abbey continued for centuries.
free-imperial-city-of-kempten.r: A council of guilds and patricians governed the small walled town, which lived from crafts, linen and trade on the Iller. In 1525, in the so-called Great Purchase, the town bought out the abbot's remaining rights over it. It adopted the Reformation, becoming a Lutheran island beside the Catholic abbey town. Both towns were damaged in the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-kempten.e: Bavaria annexed the imperial city in 1802 and the abbey in 1803, and in 1818 the two were united into one town. Kempten is now a Bavarian city, and its old imperial town and abbey quarter remain distinct.

french-ionian-islands.t: Ionian Islands under French rule after the fall of Venice, twice annexed by France between 1797 and 1814 and finally held only at Corfu.
french-ionian-islands.o: Napoleon's destruction of the Republic of Venice in 1797 brought French troops to Corfu. The Treaty of Campo Formio in October 1797 gave France the Venetian Ionian Islands and their mainland outposts, which were organised as three French departments: Corcyre, Ithaque and Mer-Egee.
french-ionian-islands.r: The French burned the Golden Book of the Venetian nobility, planted liberty trees and introduced revolutionary institutions, but their requisitions and anticlericalism alienated many islanders. A Russian-Ottoman expedition under Admiral Ushakov took the islands in 1799, creating the Septinsular Republic. The Treaty of Tilsit in 1807 returned them to France.
french-ionian-islands.e: Britain blockaded and captured most of the islands in 1809-1810, but the French governor General Donzelot held Corfu until it was surrendered in 1814 after Napoleon's abdication. The islands then became the United States of the Ionian Islands under British protection.

free-imperial-city-of-wimpfen.t: A small imperial city on the Neckar, built beside the largest Hohenstaufen palace, that kept its freedom until 1803.
free-imperial-city-of-wimpfen.o: Wimpfen stands on a hill above the Neckar near a Roman fort. Around 1200 the Hohenstaufen built their largest imperial palace there, and the town that grew beside it received town rights. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen, Wimpfen counted as a free imperial city by about 1300, while Wimpfen im Tal below kept its collegiate church of Saint Peter.
free-imperial-city-of-wimpfen.r: A council of burghers ran the city and its tiny territory, which lived from Neckar shipping, crafts and farming. The town adopted Lutheranism in the 16th century, though the collegiate foundation in the valley stayed Catholic. In 1622 the Battle of Wimpfen was fought nearby, a victory for Tilly's Catholic League army over Margrave George Frederick of Baden-Durlach.
free-imperial-city-of-wimpfen.e: In the mediatisation of 1802 and 1803 Wimpfen passed briefly to Baden and then to Hesse-Darmstadt, remaining a Hessian exclave until after the Second World War. Salt springs found in 1817 made it a spa, and as Bad Wimpfen it is now part of Baden-Württemberg.

french-congo.t: France's colony north of the Congo River, founded through Brazza's treaties and notorious for its concession-company abuses.
french-congo.o: In 1880 Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signed a treaty with the Makoko, ruler of the Kingdom of Tio, placing land north of the Congo River under French protection; Brazzaville grew from his post. The Berlin Conference of 1884-1885 recognised French claims, and the territories were united with Gabon as the colony of Gabon-Congo, renamed French Congo in 1891.
french-congo.r: Brazza was commissioner-general until 1897, ruling with few resources from Libreville. From 1899 the government handed most of the land to about forty concession companies, which forced Africans to collect rubber and ivory, leading to scandals and depopulation. A commission led by Brazza investigated the abuses in 1905.
french-congo.e: In 1903 the colony was divided into Gabon, Middle Congo and Ubangi-Shari-Chad, and in 1910 these were organised as French Equatorial Africa.

free-imperial-city-of-metz.t: A self-governing patrician republic in Lorraine, one of the richest cities of the Empire, which France seized and held against Charles V in 1552.
free-imperial-city-of-metz.o: The citizens of Metz gradually took power from their bishops during the 12th century, and by the late 12th century the city governed itself under the emperor's protection, outside the Prince-Bishopric of Metz. A master-échevin elected each year headed the city government from 1180.
free-imperial-city-of-metz.r: Metz was run by the paraiges, a handful of patrician family associations that monopolised offices. Its merchants and bankers lent money to princes across the region, and the city controlled a sizable rural territory. Metz fought the dukes of Lorraine and withstood a siege by Charles VII and René of Anjou in 1444.
free-imperial-city-of-metz.e: In 1552 Henry II of France occupied Metz under the Treaty of Chambord with German Protestant princes. Charles V besieged it in the winter of 1552–1553 but Francis of Guise held it. Metz became French, which the Peace of Westphalia confirmed in 1648.

free-state-of-thuringia.t: Union of seven small Thuringian states in 1920, which saw the first Nazi minister and later disappeared into East German districts.
free-state-of-thuringia.o: After 1918 the small Ernestine and Schwarzburg states and Reuss sought union. On 1 May 1920 Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, Saxe-Meiningen, Saxe-Altenburg, Saxe-Gotha, Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt, Schwarzburg-Sondershausen and the People's State of Reuss merged into the Land of Thuringia, with Weimar as capital. Coburg chose Bavaria instead.
free-state-of-thuringia.r: Thuringia had textile, toy, glass and optical industries, including Carl Zeiss in Jena. In 1923 a left-wing government was removed by the federal army. The Bauhaus left Weimar for Dessau in 1925 under nationalist pressure. In 1930 Wilhelm Frick became Thuringia's interior minister, the first Nazi to hold a ministerial post. Buchenwald concentration camp was built near Weimar in 1937.
free-state-of-thuringia.e: After 1945 Thuringia was in the Soviet zone and became a Land of the German Democratic Republic. In 1952 it was divided into the districts of Erfurt, Gera and Suhl; the state was re-established in 1990.

free-imperial-city-of-aachen.t: Charlemagne's favourite residence and the coronation city of German kings for six centuries, a free imperial city until the French annexed it.
free-imperial-city-of-aachen.o: Charlemagne built his palace and the Palatine Chapel at Aachen, around hot springs, and was buried there in 814. Otto I was crowned in the chapel in 936, beginning a tradition of royal coronations. In 1166 Frederick Barbarossa, having had Charlemagne canonised in 1165, granted the town a charter of liberties.
free-imperial-city-of-aachen.r: Aachen was governed by a council of patricians and guild representatives. Some thirty German kings were crowned there until 1531. Its economy rested on cloth and brass making, as well as pilgrimage to relics shown every seven years. A great fire in 1656 destroyed much of the city, and later spas attracted European visitors.
free-imperial-city-of-aachen.e: The city hosted peace congresses in 1668 and 1748. French revolutionary troops occupied it in 1794, and it was formally annexed by France under the Treaty of Lunéville in 1801. In 1815 it became Prussian. Aachen Cathedral was among the first World Heritage Sites.
