firdafylke.t: Petty kingdom of the western Norwegian fjords of Sunnfjord and Nordfjord, one of the realms conquered by Harald Fairhair.
firdafylke.o: Firdafylke, the land of the fjord districts between Sogn and Møre, is known almost entirely from Snorri Sturluson's sagas. It appears as one of the small coastal kingdoms of western Norway in the century before unification.
firdafylke.r: Little is recorded beyond the sagas. Its people farmed the narrow fjord valleys and fished the coast, and like neighbouring fylki it had its own assembly. Many families from the district later took part in the settlement of Iceland.
firdafylke.e: According to Heimskringla, its king Audbjørn fell fighting Harald Fairhair at the Battle of Solskjel, and the district then passed under Harald's earls. It became part of the Kingdom of Norway and of the Gulating law province.

free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-hall.t: Salt-producing imperial city on the Kocher that gave its name to the heller coin and became an early stronghold of the Reformation under Johannes Brenz.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-hall.o: Hall grew around salt springs on the Kocher, worked since Celtic times. Its mint produced the Haller pfennig, or heller, from the 12th century. The town was a Hohenstaufen possession, and in 1280 King Rudolf I confirmed its independence from local lords, establishing it as an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-hall.r: Patrician families who owned shares in the salt works dominated the council until guilds gained seats in the early 16th century. Salt boiling provided most of the city's wealth. Hall built a sizeable rural territory, buying Limpurg castle in 1541. From 1522 the preacher Johannes Brenz led a moderate Lutheran Reformation that influenced much of south-western Germany.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-hall.e: The city was annexed by Württemberg in 1802, and the salt works became a state enterprise. It is now a town in Baden-Württemberg, its old town and the great steps of St. Michael's Church well preserved.

free-imperial-city-of-windsheim.t: Small Franconian imperial city on the Aisch, surrounded by Hohenzollern lands, which adopted the Reformation and kept its freedom until 1802.
free-imperial-city-of-windsheim.o: Windsheim grew from a Frankish royal estate and later belonged to the bishops of Würzburg before returning to the Empire. It was recognised as an imperial city in the mid 13th century, around 1248, on the road between Nuremberg and Würzburg.
free-imperial-city-of-windsheim.r: The town was governed by a council and lived from farming, wine, crafts and its market. It was surrounded by the lands of the Hohenzollern margraves of Ansbach, on whom it depended for trade and with whom it often quarrelled. Windsheim adopted the Reformation in the 1520s and signed the Augsburg Confession in 1530.
free-imperial-city-of-windsheim.e: The city lost its freedom when it was annexed by Bavaria in 1802. Its saline springs later made it a spa, renamed Bad Windsheim, and it now hosts the Franconian Open-Air Museum of rural buildings.

free-city-of-riga.t: The largest Hanseatic city of Livonia, which fought the Livonian Order and its archbishops for its liberties until it submitted to Poland in 1581.
free-city-of-riga.o: Riga was founded by Bishop Albert in 1201 and soon received its own town law. By the late 13th century its merchant council was strong enough to act independently, and it joined the Hanseatic League in 1282, controlling trade along the Daugava with Polotsk and Lithuania.
free-city-of-riga.r: The city was governed by a council of merchants, with guilds for merchants and craftsmen. Its rivalry with the Livonian Order led to open war from 1297; the city even allied with pagan Lithuania, but the Order captured it in 1330. Riga exported furs, wax, flax and timber and adopted Lutheranism in 1522, one of the first cities outside Germany to do so.
free-city-of-riga.e: When Terra Mariana collapsed in 1561, Riga refused to submit and remained a free city for twenty years. In 1581 it accepted the rule of Stephen Báthory of Poland-Lithuania, and it later became the capital of Swedish Livonia and then of the Governorate of Livonia.

free-imperial-city-of-dortmund.t: Westphalian imperial city on the Hellweg, a leading Hanseatic town that held off Cologne in the Great Feud of 1388 to 1389.
free-imperial-city-of-dortmund.o: Dortmund grew around a royal court on the Hellweg, the trade road between the Rhine and the Weser. Ottonian kings held assemblies there, and by around 1220 it was the only imperial city in Westphalia. Its merchants traded across the North Sea and Baltic, and it became a leading member of the Hanseatic League.
free-imperial-city-of-dortmund.r: A council of merchant patricians ruled the city. Its free court was the leading tribunal of the Vehmic courts of Westphalia. In the Great Dortmund Feud of 1388 to 1389 it withstood a siege by the Archbishop of Cologne and the Count of the Mark. The city was surrounded by Mark territory and gradually lost trade. Lutheranism was introduced in the 1560s and 1570s.
free-imperial-city-of-dortmund.e: In 1803 Dortmund lost its freedom and was given to the house of Nassau-Orange. It belonged to the Grand Duchy of Berg from 1808 and to Prussia from 1815, growing into a great coal and steel city of the Ruhr.

free-state-of-brunswick.t: Republican successor of the Duchy of Brunswick, remembered for giving Adolf Hitler German citizenship in 1932.
free-state-of-brunswick.o: Duke Ernest Augustus abdicated on 8 November 1918, and a socialist republic was proclaimed in Brunswick. After a period of councils and unrest, a constitution was adopted in 1922, making Brunswick a parliamentary free state.
free-state-of-brunswick.r: Brunswick had industry, canning and the Büssing vehicle works, and its politics were polarised between Social Democrats and the right. From 1930 the Nazis shared government, and in February 1932 the Nazi interior minister Dietrich Klagges appointed Adolf Hitler to a nominal post in the state's Berlin legation, which made the stateless Hitler a German citizen and allowed him to run for president.
free-state-of-brunswick.e: After 1945 Brunswick was in the British zone. In November 1946 it was merged with Hanover, Oldenburg and Schaumburg-Lippe into the new state of Lower Saxony.

federation-of-south-arabia.t: Britain's last attempt to build a friendly state around Aden, which collapsed under nationalist insurgency in 1967.
federation-of-south-arabia.o: In April 1962 the Federation of Arab Emirates of the South was renamed the Federation of South Arabia. In January 1963 the Colony of Aden joined as the State of Aden, despite opposition from Aden's trade unions and nationalists, and more protectorate states joined in the following years.
federation-of-south-arabia.r: The federation was ruled by sultans, emirs and sheikhs with British advisers, and Britain kept its military base at Aden. In December 1963 a grenade attack on the High Commissioner at Aden airport led to a state of emergency. Two rival movements, the National Liberation Front and FLOSY, fought the British and each other in Aden and the Radfan mountains.
federation-of-south-arabia.e: In 1966 Britain announced it would leave without a defence agreement. In 1967 the federal army and states collapsed as the National Liberation Front took over; Britain withdrew on 29 November 1967 and South Yemen became independent.

free-imperial-city-of-nordlingen.t: Walled Swabian imperial city inside the Ries meteorite crater, known for its Whitsun fair and the two battles of Nördlingen in the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-nordlingen.o: A royal estate at Nördlingen in the Ries basin, an ancient meteorite crater, passed to the bishop of Regensburg and back to the Hohenstaufen. In 1215 Emperor Frederick II recognised it as an imperial city, and its growth was helped by its position on the roads between Franconia, Swabia and Bavaria.
free-imperial-city-of-nordlingen.r: A council dominated by merchants ruled the city. Its Whitsun fair was one of the leading markets of southern Germany, and cloth, leather and furs were its main trades. Nördlingen adopted the Reformation in the 1520s. The great hall church of St. Georg, with its tall tower known as the Daniel, and an intact ring of walls testify to its wealth.
free-imperial-city-of-nordlingen.e: The city suffered in the Thirty Years War, when imperial and Spanish troops won the first Battle of Nördlingen in 1634 and French forces fought there again in 1645. It lost its freedom in 1803 to the Electorate of Bavaria.

free-city-of-krakow.t: A small city republic around Krakow under the joint protection of Austria, Prussia and Russia, the last free remnant of Poland.
free-city-of-krakow.o: Unable to agree who should have Krakow, the powers at the Congress of Vienna in 1815 made the city and its surrounding district a free, independent and strictly neutral city under the protection of Austria, Prussia and Russia.
free-city-of-krakow.r: Krakow had a senate, an assembly and its own constitution, though the three protecting powers supervised it through their residents. It was the only place where Polish institutions functioned freely, and the Jagiellonian University was a centre of Polish culture. Its free-trade status helped commerce, and it became a refuge for Polish patriots and conspirators.
free-city-of-krakow.e: In February 1846 a national uprising broke out in Krakow and quickly collapsed. In November 1846 Austria annexed the city with the agreement of Prussia and Russia, joining it to the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria as the Grand Duchy of Krakow.

free-imperial-city-of-gengenbach.t: A small Black Forest imperial city in the Kinzig valley that grew around a Benedictine abbey and kept its freedom until 1803.
free-imperial-city-of-gengenbach.o: Gengenbach grew around a Benedictine abbey founded in the 8th century. The town received its rights under the Hohenstaufen and in the 14th century became a free imperial city, recognised by Charles IV in 1360. With Zell am Harmersbach and Offenburg it lay within the imperial bailiwick of the Ortenau, which emperors often pledged to neighbouring princes.
free-imperial-city-of-gengenbach.r: A council of burghers governed the town, whose economy rested on wine, timber, crafts and traffic along the Kinzig valley route through the Black Forest. Relations with the abbey were often tense. Gengenbach briefly accepted the Reformation but returned to Catholicism. French troops burned it in 1689 during the Nine Years' War, and it was rebuilt in Baroque style.
free-imperial-city-of-gengenbach.e: In 1803 the mediatisation gave Gengenbach and its neighbours to Baden, which became the Grand Duchy of Baden in 1806. Its half-timbered old town, walls and town hall survive.

free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck.t: The Queen of the Hanse, a Baltic port whose law and merchants shaped dozens of towns from Tallinn to Gdańsk and which stayed a free state until 1937.
free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck.o: Henry the Lion refounded Lübeck on the Trave in 1159 as a German port to the Baltic. After his fall the town came under the emperor, and in 1226 Frederick II granted it the status of a free imperial city. Its merchants soon led the Hanseatic League, which held its diets in Lübeck.
free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck.r: A council of merchant families ruled the city, and Lübeck law was adopted by about a hundred Baltic towns. Wealth came from trade in herring, salt, grain, furs and timber, visible in the Holstentor and St. Mary's Church. Lübeck turned Lutheran in 1530, and under the mayor Jürgen Wullenwever it waged the disastrous Count's Feud against Denmark in 1534 to 1536.
free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck.e: As the Hanse faded Lübeck declined. It was annexed by France from 1811 to 1813, then joined the German Confederation and German Empire as a city-state. The Greater Hamburg Act of 1937 merged it into Prussia. Its old town is a World Heritage Site.

free-state-of-bavaria.t: Bavaria as a republic, from the 1918 revolution through the Nazi era to a prosperous and self-confident state of modern Germany.
free-state-of-bavaria.o: On 7 November 1918 the Independent Socialist Kurt Eisner proclaimed the Free State of Bavaria in Munich, ending the Wittelsbach monarchy. Eisner was assassinated in February 1919, and a short-lived Bavarian Soviet Republic was crushed that spring. The Bamberg constitution of 1919 established Bavaria as a parliamentary free state.
free-state-of-bavaria.r: Inter-war Bavaria became a conservative stronghold and refuge of the extreme right, where Hitler's Beer Hall Putsch failed in 1923. After 1933 the Nazis took control and Munich became the capital of the movement. After 1945 Bavaria was in the American zone; its 1946 constitution created a state long dominated by the Christian Social Union, which built a high-technology economy.
free-state-of-bavaria.e: Bavaria joined the Federal Republic of Germany in 1949, though its Landtag rejected the Basic Law while accepting its validity. It remains one of Germany's sixteen states, with Munich as capital.

french-fourth-republic.t: France's post-war parliamentary republic, unstable in government but launching European integration and rapid economic growth before collapsing over Algeria.
french-fourth-republic.o: After the Provisional Government of the French Republic, voters approved a new constitution in October 1946. It created a strong National Assembly and a weak president; Vincent Auriol was the first. The colonies were reorganised as the French Union.
french-fourth-republic.r: Coalitions changed constantly, with more than twenty governments in twelve years. Yet economic modernisation was rapid, guided by Jean Monnet's planning. Robert Schuman proposed the European Coal and Steel Community in 1950, and France signed the Treaty of Rome in 1957. Defeat at Dien Bien Phu ended the Indochina war in 1954, and Pierre Mendès France negotiated the withdrawal.
french-fourth-republic.e: The Algerian War, begun in 1954, divided the nation. In May 1958 army officers and settlers seized power in Algiers, and parliament called back Charles de Gaulle, who drew up a new constitution creating the French Fifth Republic.

free-imperial-city-of-ulm.t: Danube imperial city of fustian weavers and merchants, builder of the minster with the world's tallest church spire and a leader of the Swabian League.
free-imperial-city-of-ulm.o: Ulm grew around a royal palace at the meeting of the Blau and the Danube, recorded from 854. It was a favoured Hohenstaufen town, and after their fall it was confirmed as an imperial city, its privileges renewed by Rudolf I in 1274.
free-imperial-city-of-ulm.r: The Schwörbrief of 1397 gave the guilds a majority on the council, and the mayor swore an annual oath to the citizens. Fustian weaving and the Danube trade made Ulm rich, and it acquired the largest territory of any imperial city after Nuremberg. Its citizens began the minster in 1377. Ulm led the Swabian city leagues and the Swabian League, and turned Protestant in 1530 to 1531.
free-imperial-city-of-ulm.e: Ulm lost its freedom to Bavaria in 1802 and passed to Württemberg in 1810; Napoleon defeated an Austrian army there in 1805. The minster spire was completed in 1890, and Albert Einstein was born in Ulm in 1879.

fadhli-sultanate.t: A tribal sultanate on the Abyan coast east of Aden, a member of the British-backed south Arabian federation until 1967.
fadhli-sultanate.o: The Fadhli tribe held the coastal plain of Abyan and the hills behind it. In the late 17th century, as the Qasimid State lost its hold over the south, the Fadhli chiefs established an independent sultanate, with Shuqra on the coast as its chief town.
fadhli-sultanate.r: The sultans governed through tribal custom, controlling routes between Aden and the interior. In the 19th century they often raided the outskirts of British Aden before signing a protection treaty with Britain, becoming part of the Aden Protectorate. From the 1940s the Abyan irrigation scheme turned the delta into a cotton-growing area, bringing new revenue. The sultanate joined the Federation of Arab Emirates of the South in 1959.
fadhli-sultanate.e: It was a member of the Federation of South Arabia until 1967, when the National Liberation Front took over the territory, abolished the sultanate and incorporated it into South Yemen.

fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The Hyksos kings of Avaris, rulers of Levantine origin who governed northern Egypt for about a century.
fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Around 1650 BCE rulers of Levantine descent, called Hyksos from the Egyptian for 'rulers of foreign lands', took power at Avaris in the eastern Delta and captured Memphis, ending the Middle Kingdom of Egypt. Later Egyptian tradition portrayed this as an invasion, but it grew from a long-settled Canaanite population in the Delta.
fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The Hyksos adopted pharaonic titles and Egyptian administration while keeping Levantine customs at Avaris, where their great palaces and temples have been excavated. They worshipped Seth, identified with the storm god Baal, and traded widely with Canaan and Cyprus. Their era spread the horse and chariot in Egypt, and the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus was copied under Apepi. Khyan's name appears on objects found as far as Knossos and Baghdad.
fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: The Seventeenth Dynasty of Egypt at Thebes went to war against Apepi. Around 1550 BCE Ahmose I captured Avaris and then besieged Sharuhen in southern Canaan, driving out the Hyksos and founding the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom.

free-imperial-city-of-pfullendorf.t: Small Swabian imperial city north of Lake Constance, chartered by Frederick II in 1220 and a modest Catholic member of the Swabian city leagues.
free-imperial-city-of-pfullendorf.o: Pfullendorf was the seat of counts whose lands passed to the Hohenstaufen in the later 12th century. In 1220 Emperor Frederick II granted the town its charter, and it became an imperial city on the roads between the Danube and Lake Constance.
free-imperial-city-of-pfullendorf.r: The town was governed by a council with guild participation and lived from linen weaving, crafts and its market for the surrounding countryside. Its small territory included a few villages. It joined the Swabian city leagues and later the Swabian imperial circle, but remained a minor power, and it stayed Catholic during the Reformation.
free-imperial-city-of-pfullendorf.e: Pfullendorf lost its imperial freedom in 1803 when it was annexed by the Margraviate of Baden, soon the Grand Duchy of Baden. It is now a small town in Baden-Württemberg with a well-preserved old centre and parts of its medieval walls.

free-imperial-city-of-donauworth.t: A Swabian imperial city on the Danube whose sectarian riot of 1606 and seizure by Bavaria helped set Europe on the road to the Thirty Years' War.
free-imperial-city-of-donauworth.o: Donauwörth grew where the Wörnitz meets the Danube, beside the Holy Cross abbey and a castle. A Hohenstaufen possession, it later fell under the dukes of Bavaria, from whom it repeatedly bought back its freedom. It counted as an imperial city from about 1301, although it was pledged to Bavaria again from 1376 until 1434.
free-imperial-city-of-donauworth.r: A council of burghers governed the town, which prospered from Danube trade and the road between Nuremberg and Augsburg. Most citizens became Lutheran, while the Benedictine Holy Cross abbey kept a Catholic minority. In 1606 Protestant townspeople attacked a Catholic procession, and the Imperial Aulic Council placed the city under the imperial ban.
free-imperial-city-of-donauworth.e: Duke Maximilian I of Bavaria executed the ban in 1607, occupied Donauwörth, re-Catholicised it and in 1609 annexed it. Alarmed Protestant princes formed the Protestant Union in 1608, and the Catholic League answered in 1609. The town has remained Bavarian ever since.

fourth-brazilian-republic.t: Brazil's democratic Populist Republic, the era of Petrobras and Brasília, which ended with the military coup of 1964.
fourth-brazilian-republic.o: After the fall of the Estado Novo (Brazil) in 1945, General Eurico Gaspar Dutra was elected president, and a new democratic constitution was adopted in 1946. It restored Congress, parties and elections, though illiterate people could not vote.
fourth-brazilian-republic.r: Getúlio Vargas returned as elected president in 1950 and founded Petrobras, the state oil company, in 1953. Facing a political crisis, he shot himself in 1954. Juscelino Kubitschek promised 'fifty years in five' and built the new capital, Brasília, inaugurated in 1960. Jânio Quadros resigned within months in 1961, and the military accepted his vice-president João Goulart only under a temporary parliamentary system.
fourth-brazilian-republic.e: Goulart's proposals for land reform and his ties to the left alarmed the military, the middle classes and the United States. A coup on 31 March and 1 April 1964 deposed him and began the Brazilian military dictatorship.

free-imperial-city-of-muhlhausen.t: Thuringian imperial city famous as the base of Thomas Müntzer during the Peasants' War and for one of the oldest law books written in German.
free-imperial-city-of-muhlhausen.o: Mühlhausen grew around a royal palace and was favoured by the Hohenstaufen emperors, gaining the status of an imperial city by about 1180. Around 1200 to 1230 its law was set down in the Mühlhausen Reichsrechtsbuch, one of the earliest legal texts in German.
free-imperial-city-of-muhlhausen.r: A council of patricians and later guild representatives ruled the city, which grew rich from cloth, woad and trade, joined the Hanseatic League and allied with Erfurt and Nordhausen in a Thuringian city league. In 1525 the radical preacher Thomas Müntzer made Mühlhausen his base, set up the Eternal League and led its men to defeat at Frankenhausen in the Peasants' War.
free-imperial-city-of-muhlhausen.e: After 1525 the city lost its freedom for two decades under Saxon and Hessian control, regaining imperial status in 1548. It was annexed by Prussia in 1802, belonged to the Kingdom of Westphalia from 1807 to 1813, and then returned to Prussia; it is now in Thuringia.

fidach.t: A Pictish province named in the legend of the seven sons of Cruithne, of uncertain location, perhaps around Moray and Ross.
fidach.o: Fidach is known only from medieval lists of the seven Pictish provinces, which named them after legendary sons of Cruithne, the father of the Picts. Its location is not stated, and historians have suggested Moray, Ross or the area around the Moray Firth.
fidach.r: Nothing is known of its rulers, society or government beyond its inclusion in the province lists. It was presumably one of the regional territories of Pictland, subject to the kings of the Picts.
fidach.e: Like the other provinces, it disappeared as a distinct unit when Pictland was absorbed into the Kingdom of Scotland in the 9th and 10th centuries.

free-province-of-guayaquil.t: The independent port province of Guayaquil, freed in 1820, whose fate was settled when Bolívar annexed it on the eve of his meeting with San Martín.
free-province-of-guayaquil.o: On 9 October 1820 a group of patriots in Guayaquil, the main port of the Royal Audiencia of Quito, overthrew the Spanish authorities. A cabildo declared the Free Province of Guayaquil, with the poet José Joaquín de Olmedo as head of government.
free-province-of-guayaquil.r: The province adopted a provisional regulation of government and created an army, the Protective Division of Quito, to free the highlands. Its first campaigns failed, but with troops sent by Bolívar under Antonio José de Sucre, and Peruvian reinforcements, the patriots won at Pichincha in May 1822. Guayaquil's elite was divided over joining Gran Colombia, Peru or staying independent.
free-province-of-guayaquil.e: Bolívar entered Guayaquil in July 1822 and annexed it to Gran Colombia; Olmedo left in protest. Days later Bolívar met San Martín in the Guayaquil Conference. Guayaquil became part of the Republic of Ecuador in 1830.

free-imperial-city-of-turckheim.t: A walled Alsatian wine town, the smallest member of the Decapolis, near which Turenne won a decisive battle for France in 1675.
free-imperial-city-of-turckheim.o: Turckheim grew at the entrance to the Fecht valley near Colmar, on lands long linked to the abbey of Munster. Walled in the early 14th century, it was recognised as an imperial city around 1312 and in 1354 joined the Decapolis, the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities.
free-imperial-city-of-turckheim.r: A council of burghers ruled the town, whose wealth came almost wholly from its vineyards; its three gates and much of its wall survive. It remained Catholic during the Reformation. The round of the night watchman, still re-enacted in summer, recalls the town's tradition of guarding its own walls.
free-imperial-city-of-turckheim.e: After 1648 the Decapolis came under French protection. On 5 January 1675 Marshal Turenne defeated the imperial army at the Battle of Turckheim, securing Alsace, and the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1679 confirmed annexation by the Kingdom of France. It is now in the Haut-Rhin department.

france-antarctique.t: A short-lived French colony in Guanabara Bay whose destruction by the Portuguese led directly to the founding of Rio de Janeiro.
france-antarctique.o: In 1555 the French admiral Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon, backed by Admiral Gaspard de Coligny, sailed to Guanabara Bay in Brazil with some 600 settlers. They built Fort Coligny on a small island and allied with the Tupinambá, who traded brazilwood with French merchants.
france-antarctique.r: The colony was intended partly as a refuge for French Protestants, and a group of Calvinists sent from Geneva arrived in 1557, including Jean de Léry, whose account of the Tupinambá became a classic of travel writing. Villegaignon, however, quarrelled with them over doctrine and expelled them, and some were executed. Harsh discipline and desertions weakened the settlement.
france-antarctique.e: Governor-general Mem de Sá destroyed Fort Coligny in 1560. His nephew Estácio de Sá founded Rio de Janeiro in 1565 and, with Portuguese and Temiminó forces, drove the remaining French and their Tupinambá allies from the bay by 1567.

free-cities-of-menton-and-roquebrune.t: Two Riviera towns that broke away from Monaco in 1848 over taxes on their lemons and lived as free cities until France bought them.
free-cities-of-menton-and-roquebrune.o: Menton and Roquebrune formed most of the Principality of Monaco's territory and income, through their lemon and olive trade. Resentment at Prince Florestan I's taxes and monopolies boiled over in 1848, and in March the two towns declared themselves free cities under the protection of the Kingdom of Sardinia.
free-cities-of-menton-and-roquebrune.r: The towns governed themselves through elected councils, with Sardinian troops present. A plebiscite favoured union with Sardinia, but it was never formally completed because of diplomatic objections. Their economy remained based on citrus fruit, and Menton began to attract winter visitors.
free-cities-of-menton-and-roquebrune.e: After Sardinia ceded Nice to France in 1860, Menton and Roquebrune voted to join France. In 1861 Prince Charles III of Monaco sold his rights to Napoleon III's Second French Empire for four million francs.

free-imperial-city-of-esslingen.t: Wine town on the Neckar that was a leading Swabian imperial city, founding place of the Swabian League and a lasting rival of Württemberg.
free-imperial-city-of-esslingen.o: Esslingen grew around a shrine of Saint Vitalis and a bridge over the Neckar, gaining market rights in the Carolingian period. The Hohenstaufen favoured the town, and it was treated as an imperial city by the early 13th century, its privileges confirmed by Frederick II around 1219.
free-imperial-city-of-esslingen.r: A council of patricians and guilds governed the town, which prospered from wine, cloth and bridge tolls. Its position next to Württemberg led to repeated wars with the counts of Württemberg in the 14th and 15th centuries. In 1488 the Swabian League was founded at Esslingen, and the city hosted the imperial governing council in the 1520s. It adopted the Reformation in 1531.
free-imperial-city-of-esslingen.e: Esslingen lost its freedom in 1802 when it was annexed by Württemberg, its old enemy. It became an industrial town known for machine building and remains in Baden-Württemberg, with its Gothic churches and old town hall.

finnish-democratic-republic.t: Soviet puppet government created for Finland at the start of the Winter War, led by Otto Wille Kuusinen and abandoned in 1940.
finnish-democratic-republic.o: On 30 November 1939 the Soviet Union invaded Finland. The next day it announced the formation of the Finnish Democratic Republic, nominally based in the border town of Terijoki, with the exiled Finnish communist Otto Wille Kuusinen as head. The Soviet Union recognised it as Finland's only legitimate government and signed a treaty of mutual assistance with it.
finnish-democratic-republic.r: The 'Terijoki government' existed mainly on paper and was run from Moscow. It raised a Finnish People's Army from Soviet Finns and Karelians, intended to enter Helsinki behind the Red Army. Finns overwhelmingly rejected it, and it helped unite Finnish society behind its real government.
finnish-democratic-republic.e: Finnish resistance forced the Soviet Union to negotiate with the Helsinki government. The Moscow Peace Treaty of March 1940 ended the war, and the puppet government was quietly dissolved. Its leaders and territory were merged into the new Karelo-Finnish Soviet Socialist Republic, with Kuusinen as its head.

frisian-kingdom.t: Pagan kingdom of the North Sea coast, ruler of the trading port of Dorestad, which resisted the Franks for over a century.
frisian-kingdom.o: After the Roman period the coastal Low Countries were resettled from the 5th century, and by around 600 the Frisians held a realm stretching along the coast from the Zwin to the Weser, later called Magna Frisia. Its first known king, Aldgisl, sheltered the English bishop Wilfrid in 678.
frisian-kingdom.r: The Frisians were seafaring traders whose merchants carried cloth, slaves and goods across the North Sea, and their emporium of Dorestad on the Rhine was one of the busiest ports in north-west Europe. Their silver sceattas circulated widely. King Redbad opposed the Christian mission of Willibrord.
frisian-kingdom.e: Pippin of Herstal defeated Redbad around 690 and took Dorestad and Utrecht, but Redbad recovered much ground before his death in 719. In 734 Charles Martel defeated and killed King Poppo at the Boarn, and Frisia was absorbed into the Kingdom of the Franks.

free-imperial-city-of-wangen.t: Small Catholic imperial city in the western Allgäu, a market for linen and scythes that kept its freedom until 1802.
free-imperial-city-of-wangen.o: Wangen grew around a settlement linked to the Imperial Abbey of Saint Gall, which held rights there from the 9th century. The Hohenstaufen developed the town, and after their fall it was recognised as an imperial city by Rudolf I in 1286.
free-imperial-city-of-wangen.r: A council of burghers ruled the town and its small territory. Linen weaving, scythe making and the market for the western Allgäu were its main trades. Wangen remained Catholic during the Reformation and was a member of the Swabian imperial circle. It suffered heavily in the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-wangen.e: Wangen lost its freedom to Bavaria in 1802 and passed to Württemberg in 1810. It is now a town in Baden-Württemberg with a well-preserved old centre, gate towers and painted houses.

five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.t: Five fortified Danish towns of the east Midlands, Derby, Leicester, Lincoln, Nottingham and Stamford, that formed the core of Viking rule south of the Humber.
five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.o: After the Great Heathen Army partitioned Mercia in 877, Danish warbands settled the east Midlands around fortified centres. Each borough was the base of a jarl and his army, controlling the surrounding district, in an area later known as part of the Danelaw.
five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.r: The boroughs were military and trading centres that grew into towns, with Danish law, land units and many Scandinavian place-names in -by and -thorpe. They acted together at times, but there is no evidence of a single ruler. The settlers soon adopted Christianity.
five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.e: Aethelflaed of Mercia and Edward the Elder took Derby, Leicester, Nottingham and Stamford between 917 and 920. After a Norse revival from York, Edmund of England recovered the Five Boroughs in 942, an event celebrated in a poem in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. The region kept distinct legal customs into the 11th century.

frankish-kingdom-of-soissons.t: Merovingian kingdom of Chlothar I, who from his base at Soissons gradually reunited all the Frankish lands.
frankish-kingdom-of-soissons.o: When Clovis died in 511, his youngest son Chlothar I received the old Frankish heartland in the north, between the Somme and the Scheldt, ruling from Soissons, the former seat of the Domain of Soissons.
frankish-kingdom-of-soissons.r: Chlothar was the most ruthless of Clovis' sons. In 524 he personally killed two of his young nephews to seize part of the Kingdom of Orléans. He shared in the conquest of the Kingdom of the Burgundians and of Thuringia, where he took the princess Radegund as his wife.
frankish-kingdom-of-soissons.e: Through the deaths of his brothers and nephew, Chlothar inherited Austrasia in 555 and Paris in 558, reuniting the Kingdom of the Franks. He died in 561 and was buried at Saint-Médard in Soissons. His son Chilperic I received Soissons, the core of Neustria.

faroese-commonwealth.t: Self-governing Norse community of the Faroe Islands, ruled by its assembly at Tinganes until it came under the Norwegian crown.
faroese-commonwealth.o: Norse settlers reached the Faroe Islands in the early 9th century; the Irish monk Dicuil wrote around 825 that Irish hermits there had been driven out by Northmen raiders. The settlers were farmers and herders, many from western Norway, and some with Gaelic links from the British Isles.
faroese-commonwealth.r: The islanders governed themselves through the Alting at Tinganes, in what is now Tórshavn, one of the oldest parliamentary sites in the world. Sheep farming, fowling and fishing supported the population. The Færeyinga saga tells how Sigmundur Brestisson brought Christianity around 999 for King Olaf Tryggvason, opposed by the chieftain Tróndur í Gøtu.
faroese-commonwealth.e: By about 1035 the islands paid tax to the Norwegian king and became part of the Kingdom of Norway. They later passed to Denmark-Norway and remained with Denmark after 1814. The Løgting still meets in Tórshavn, and the Faroe Islands are a self-governing part of the Danish realm.

french-third-republic.t: France's longest-lasting regime since the Revolution, which built secular schools and a colonial empire, won the First World War and fell in 1940.
french-third-republic.o: After Napoleon III's capture at Sedan, Paris proclaimed the Republic on 4 September 1870. Defeat by Prussia, the loss of Alsace-Lorraine and the crushing of the Paris Commune followed. A monarchist assembly could not agree on a king, and the constitutional laws of 1875 created a parliamentary republic almost by default.
french-third-republic.r: Strong parliaments and short-lived cabinets governed. Jules Ferry's laws made primary schooling free, compulsory and secular, and the 1905 law separated church and state. The Dreyfus Affair divided the nation. France built a large empire in Africa and Indochina. It won the First World War under Georges Clemenceau at a cost of 1.4 million dead, and the Popular Front of Léon Blum introduced paid holidays in 1936.
french-third-republic.e: Germany's invasion in May 1940 brought rapid defeat. On 10 July 1940 parliament voted full powers to Marshal Pétain, ending the Republic and creating Vichy France.

free-imperial-city-of-biberach.t: Upper Swabian imperial city of fustian weavers, shared after 1648 by Catholics and Protestants, where the writer Wieland served as town clerk.
free-imperial-city-of-biberach.o: Biberach grew as a market town on the Riss under the Hohenstaufen, at the crossing of roads in Upper Swabia. After their fall, it was recognised as an imperial city by Rudolf I around 1282, on the road from Ulm to Lake Constance.
free-imperial-city-of-biberach.r: A council of patricians and guilds governed. Fustian weaving and the linen trade made Biberach prosperous in the 15th and 16th centuries. The city adopted the Reformation, but after the Thirty Years War it became a parity city in which Catholics and Lutherans shared every office and even the parish church. Christoph Martin Wieland, born nearby, served as its town clerk from 1760 to 1769.
free-imperial-city-of-biberach.e: Biberach lost its freedom in 1802 to Baden and was transferred to Württemberg in 1806. It is now a town in Baden-Württemberg, where a museum and an annual festival recall its parity tradition and Wieland.

free-imperial-city-of-landau.t: A Palatinate wine town that held imperial-city status for four centuries before Louis XIV annexed it and made it a fortress.
free-imperial-city-of-landau.o: Landau received town rights from Count Emich IV of Leiningen in 1274, and in 1291 King Rudolf I granted it the privileges of a free imperial city. In the 1320s Louis the Bavarian pledged the town to the bishops of Speyer, and Landau had to buy back its freedom, which it achieved only in 1511.
free-imperial-city-of-landau.r: A walled market town in the vineyards of the southern Palatinate, Landau was governed by a council and lived from wine, crafts and trade. From 1521 it belonged to the Decapolis, the league of Alsatian imperial cities, and it accepted the Reformation in the 16th century. Its position made it a target in every war along the upper Rhine.
free-imperial-city-of-landau.e: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 placed the Decapolis under French protection, and in 1680 Louis XIV's Chambers of Reunion annexed Landau outright; Vauban rebuilt it as a great fortress. It passed to the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1816 and is now Landau in der Pfalz in Germany.

free-imperial-city-of-buchau.t: One of the smallest free imperial cities, a town on the Federsee that shared its island site with a powerful abbey of noblewomen.
free-imperial-city-of-buchau.o: Buchau grew on an island in the Federsee in upper Swabia beside the abbey of noble canonesses founded there in the 8th century. The townspeople gradually freed themselves from the abbess's lordship, and by 1320 the town counted as a free imperial city answerable only to the emperor.
free-imperial-city-of-buchau.r: A council governed a town of a few hundred households with almost no territory, living from fishing, farming and crafts. Relations with the Imperial Abbey of Buchau next door produced constant lawsuits. The town remained Catholic and sat on the Swabian bench of cities. From the late 16th century it was home to a notable Jewish community.
free-imperial-city-of-buchau.e: In 1803 the town was mediatised and given, together with the abbey, to the princes of Thurn und Taxis; in 1806 it passed to the Kingdom of Württemberg. Now Bad Buchau, it is a spa town known for the prehistoric lake settlements of the Federsee moor.

free-hanseatic-city-of-bremen.t: Weser port and Hanseatic city that has kept its independence for more than 800 years and survives today as Germany's smallest federal state.
free-hanseatic-city-of-bremen.o: Bremen grew as the seat of the archbishops of Hamburg-Bremen. In 1186 Frederick Barbarossa granted its citizens rights that freed them from many of the archbishop's claims. Joining the Hanseatic League in the 13th century, the city slowly won self-government from the Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen, symbolised by the Roland statue of 1404.
free-hanseatic-city-of-bremen.r: A council of merchant families governed from the Gothic town hall, and wealth came from the Weser trade in grain, beer, timber and later tobacco and coffee. Bremen adopted the Reformed Protestant faith in the late 16th century. Its status as a free imperial city was confirmed by the Linz Diploma of 1646, protecting it against Swedish claims after 1648.
free-hanseatic-city-of-bremen.e: Bremen kept its freedom in 1803, was annexed by Napoleonic France from 1810 to 1813, and joined the German Confederation and German Empire as a city-state. Mayor Johann Smidt founded Bremerhaven in 1827. Since 1949 the Free Hanseatic City of Bremen has been a federal state of Germany.

free-state-of-lippe.t: Small Westphalian republic whose January 1933 election the Nazis used as a showcase just before Hitler came to power.
free-state-of-lippe.o: Prince Leopold IV abdicated on 12 November 1918, and Lippe became a free state with Detmold as capital. A constitution adopted in 1920 established a parliamentary government with a small Landtag.
free-state-of-lippe.r: Lippe was rural, with small farms, furniture making and a tradition of seasonal brickmakers. Social Democrats and liberals generally governed. In the Landtag election of 15 January 1933 the Nazis concentrated their campaign on the tiny state, with Hitler speaking repeatedly, and their gain of votes was presented as proof of momentum two weeks before he became chancellor. Under the Nazis Lippe shared a Reich governor with Schaumburg-Lippe, Alfred Meyer.
free-state-of-lippe.e: After 1945 Lippe was in the British zone. Rather than joining Lower Saxony, it opted in January 1947 to join North Rhine-Westphalia, under guarantees known as the Lippe Punctations.

falkland-islands.t: A British territory in the South Atlantic, settled by sheep farmers and claimed by Argentina as the Malvinas, which went to war over it in 1982.
falkland-islands.o: France, Britain and Spain had established rival settlements in the islands in the 18th century. In the 1820s the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata appointed Louis Vernet as governor. In January 1833 a British warship expelled the Argentine garrison, and Britain took control. A crown colony was formed in 1841, and Stanley became the capital in 1845.
falkland-islands.r: The islands developed as a sheep-farming colony, much of it owned by the Falkland Islands Company, with a small population of British descent. Port Stanley served ships rounding Cape Horn. Argentina maintained its claim. On 2 April 1982 Argentina's military government invaded; a British task force retook the islands, and Argentina surrendered on 14 June after a war that killed over 900 people.
falkland-islands.e: Fishing licences from 1987 transformed the economy. In a 2013 referendum over 99 per cent of voters chose to stay British. The islands remain a British Overseas Territory, and Argentina still claims them.

federation-of-arab-emirates-of-the-south.t: The British-sponsored union of protected states in the Aden hinterland, created in 1959 to secure Britain's base at Aden.
federation-of-arab-emirates-of-the-south.o: Facing Arab nationalism and claims by the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen, Britain encouraged the rulers of the Western Aden Protectorate to federate. On 11 February 1959 six states, the Audhali Sultanate, Emirate of Beihan, Emirate of Dhala, Fadhli Sultanate, Lower Yafa Sultanate and Upper Aulaqi Sheikhdom, signed the federation treaty with Britain.
federation-of-arab-emirates-of-the-south.r: The federation had a supreme council of rulers and a federal government at Al Ittihad, a new capital built near Aden. Britain kept responsibility for defence and foreign affairs and provided aid and the Federal Regular Army. Other states, including the Sultanate of Lahej, joined in the following years.
federation-of-arab-emirates-of-the-south.e: In April 1962 the federation was renamed the Federation of South Arabia, in preparation for the entry of the Colony of Aden in 1963.

free-imperial-city-of-worms.t: Ancient Rhine city of the Nibelungenlied, the Concordat of 1122 and Luther's defiance at the Diet of 1521, home of one of Europe's oldest Jewish communities.
free-imperial-city-of-worms.o: Worms was a Roman and Frankish centre, seat of a bishop and in legend of the Burgundian kings of the Nibelungenlied. Its citizens won growing privileges from the Salian emperors, who signed the Concordat of Worms there in 1122. Frederick Barbarossa's charter of 1184 confirmed the city's freedoms, and it gradually threw off the bishop's lordship.
free-imperial-city-of-worms.r: A council of burghers ruled, frequently in conflict with the bishop. Worms hosted many imperial diets, most famously in 1521, when Martin Luther refused to recant before Charles V. Its Jewish community, with Speyer and Mainz one of the SchUM centres of Ashkenazi learning, had a synagogue and cemetery dating from the 11th century. The city adopted Lutheranism.
free-imperial-city-of-worms.e: French troops burned Worms in 1689, and it never fully recovered. Revolutionary France annexed it in 1797. In 1816 it passed to the Grand Duchy of Hesse, and it is now in Rhineland-Palatinate, where the SchUM sites are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

first-brazilian-republic.t: Brazil's Old Republic, created by a military coup against the emperor in 1889 and dominated by the coffee and dairy oligarchies of São Paulo and Minas Gerais.
first-brazilian-republic.o: On 15 November 1889 army officers led by Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca overthrew Emperor Pedro II, a year after the abolition of slavery had cost the monarchy the support of planters. A federal constitution was adopted in 1891, giving the states wide autonomy and creating the Republic of the United States of Brazil.
first-brazilian-republic.r: After the military presidencies of Deodoro and Floriano Peixoto, civilian elites took control. São Paulo and Minas Gerais alternated the presidency in the 'coffee with milk' politics, sustained by local bosses called coronéis and limited suffrage. Coffee exports and European immigration boomed. The state crushed the religious community of Canudos in 1897. In the 1920s young officers, the tenentes, rebelled against the oligarchic system.
first-brazilian-republic.e: After the 1930 election, Getúlio Vargas of Rio Grande do Sul led the Revolution of 1930, which deposed President Washington Luís and opened the Second Brazilian Republic. Its federal structure and the power of the states left a lasting mark on Brazilian politics.

felsina.t: The leading Etruscan city of the Po valley, on the site of Bologna, until the Boii Gauls took it in the 4th century BCE.
felsina.o: Felsina grew from the Villanovan villages around modern Bologna, the area that gave the Villanovan culture its name, from the 9th century BCE. In the 6th century BCE it became a city at the centre of an Etruscan expansion north of the Apennines; Pliny called it the chief of Etruria's cities in the region.
felsina.r: Felsina controlled farmland in the Po plain and the passes over the Apennines to Etruria, and traded with the Veneti, the Celts and the Greek port of Spina. Its cemeteries, such as the Certosa, contain the bronze Certosa situla and horseshoe-shaped stone grave stelae carved with journeys to the afterlife. Little is known of its government.
felsina.e: Celtic Boii overran Felsina around the mid-4th century BCE, and the town became Bononia. Rome conquered the Boii and founded the Latin colony of Bononia in 189 BCE, from which modern Bologna descends.

free-france.t: Charles de Gaulle's government-in-exile and armed forces, which kept France in the war against Germany after 1940 and rallied much of the empire.
free-france.o: On 18 June 1940 General Charles de Gaulle, refusing the armistice, broadcast from London on the BBC calling on the French to continue fighting. Britain recognised him as leader of the Free French, and in August 1940 French Equatorial Africa, led by Félix Éboué, joined his cause.
free-france.r: Free France built an army and navy, fought at Bir Hakeim in 1942 and gathered colonies in Africa and the Pacific. A French National Committee was set up in London in 1941. De Gaulle's envoy Jean Moulin united the internal Resistance in 1943. That year the movement moved to Algiers and merged with Henri Giraud's forces in the French Committee of National Liberation.
free-france.e: In June 1944 the committee became the Provisional Government of the French Republic, which returned to Paris after its liberation in August 1944 and restored the Republic.

free-imperial-city-of-selestat.t: An Alsatian imperial city and Decapolis member, famous for its humanist Latin school and the library of Beatus Rhenanus.
free-imperial-city-of-selestat.o: Sélestat grew around a Hohenstaufen palace and the priory of Sainte-Foy on the river Ill. Frederick II made it a town in 1217, and in 1292 King Adolf of Nassau confirmed its liberties as an imperial city, answerable only to the emperor. In 1354 it was a founding member of the Decapolis, the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities.
free-imperial-city-of-selestat.r: A council drawn from the guilds ran the city, which prospered from wine, grain and river trade. In the later 15th century its Latin school became a centre of Rhineland humanism, and the scholar Beatus Rhenanus left his books to the town in 1547; they survive as the Humanist Library. The city remained Catholic during the Reformation.
free-imperial-city-of-selestat.e: Swedish troops took Sélestat in the Thirty Years' War, and after 1648 France claimed the Decapolis. Louis XIV had its walls razed in 1673, and the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1679 confirmed French rule; Vauban later refortified it. It is now a town in the Bas-Rhin department of France.

french-fifth-republic.t: The present French state, founded by de Gaulle in 1958 with a strong presidency, which ended the Algerian War and helped build the European Union.
french-fifth-republic.o: The Algerian crisis of 1958 brought down the French Fourth Republic. Charles de Gaulle returned to power and a new constitution, approved by referendum in September 1958, created a powerful presidency alongside a parliament. De Gaulle became the first president in January 1959.
french-fifth-republic.r: De Gaulle ended the Algerian War with Algerian independence in 1962, introduced direct election of the president that year, built an independent nuclear deterrent and left NATO's integrated command in 1966. The May 1968 protests shook the regime. François Mitterrand's election in 1981 brought the left to power, and periods of cohabitation followed.
french-fifth-republic.e: France remains a secular republic at the centre of the European Union, using the euro since 1999. A 2000 reform cut the presidential term to five years. Emmanuel Macron was elected president in 2017 and re-elected in 2022.

free-imperial-city-of-haguenau.t: Alsatian imperial city grown around Barbarossa's favourite palace, seat of the imperial bailiff and leading city of the Decapolis until France took it.
free-imperial-city-of-haguenau.o: Haguenau grew beside a castle of the Hohenstaufen dukes on an island in the Moder, in the great Haguenau Forest. Frederick Barbarossa granted it a charter in 1164 and rebuilt the castle as an imperial palace where the regalia were kept. After the Hohenstaufen fell, it was established as an imperial city by around 1260.
free-imperial-city-of-haguenau.r: Haguenau was seat of the imperial bailiff of Alsace and, from 1354, the leading member of the Decapolis, the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities. A council of burghers ran its affairs, with trade, forestry and crafts as its economy. In the early 16th century it was a printing centre. The city remained largely Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-haguenau.e: The Peace of Westphalia gave France rights in Alsace, and French troops burned Haguenau in 1677; the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679 confirmed French rule. It is now a town in Alsace, France.

farighunid-dynasty.t: Rulers of Guzgan in northern Afghanistan who patronised the Hudud al-Alam, the oldest surviving geography written in Persian.
farighunid-dynasty.o: The Farighunids were an Iranian dynasty ruling Guzgan (Juzjan), the region between Balkh and Merv, from at least the late 9th century. They acknowledged the Samanid Empire as overlords and were among the most prominent local princes of Khurasan.
farighunid-dynasty.r: The Farighunids were known as patrons of learning. The Hudud al-Alam, an anonymous geography of the known world completed in 982, was dedicated to the Farighunid amir Abu'l-Harith Muhammad. They kept a court in Guzgan and married into the family of the Ghaznavid ruler Sabuktigin. Their capital is uncertain, often placed at Anbar or Shiburghan.
farighunid-dynasty.e: The Farighunids transferred their loyalty from the Samanids to the Ghaznavid Empire. After the death of the last amir around 1010, Mahmud of Ghazni absorbed Guzgan into his realm.

free-state-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.t: Republican Mecklenburg-Schwerin, which replaced one of Europe's most archaic constitutions with democracy and later an early Nazi government.
free-state-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.o: Grand Duke Frederick Francis IV abdicated on 14 November 1918, and Mecklenburg-Schwerin became a free state. A constitution of 1920 created a parliamentary republic, replacing the estates-based system that had survived since 1755.
free-state-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.r: The free state remained largely agricultural, with big estates and a rural labouring population, and its capital at Schwerin. Rostock with its university and shipyards was the main town. Politics swung between Social Democrats and nationalists, and in 1932 the Nazis won a majority in the Landtag elections and formed one of the first Nazi-led state governments.
free-state-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.e: The Nazi government under Friedrich Hildebrandt dissolved parliamentary rule in 1933. On 1 January 1934 a Reich law merged it with the Free State of Mecklenburg-Strelitz into the Free State of Mecklenburg, with Schwerin as capital.

free-imperial-city-of-ravensburg.t: Upper Swabian imperial city that was home to the Great Ravensburg Trading Company, one of the leading merchant houses of late medieval Europe.
free-imperial-city-of-ravensburg.o: Ravensburg grew below the Veitsburg, ancestral castle of the Guelph dukes, where Henry the Lion may have been born. The town passed to the Hohenstaufen with the Guelph inheritance. After their line ended it became an imperial city, recognised by Rudolf I around 1276.
free-imperial-city-of-ravensburg.r: A council of patricians and guilds governed. From about 1380 to 1530 the Great Ravensburg Trading Company, owned by local families, traded linen, fustian and saffron across Spain, Italy and Flanders. Paper mills made the town an early centre of German papermaking. After the Reformation it became one of the few bi-confessional imperial cities, with Catholics and Lutherans sharing offices under the parity of 1648.
free-imperial-city-of-ravensburg.e: Ravensburg lost its freedom in 1802 to Bavaria and passed to Württemberg in 1810. It is now a town in Baden-Württemberg, known for its towers and the Ravensburger games company.

first-hellenic-republic.t: The provisional Greek state of the War of Independence, from the constitution of Epidaurus in 1822 to the arrival of a king in 1832.
first-hellenic-republic.o: In January 1822 the First National Assembly at Epidaurus declared Greek independence and adopted a provisional constitution, uniting the regional governments such as the Peloponnesian Senate. Alexandros Mavrokordatos was elected president of the executive. The new state controlled the Peloponnese, parts of the mainland and many islands.
first-hellenic-republic.r: Divided between notables, islanders and military chiefs, the government fell into civil war in 1823-1825 just as Ibrahim Pasha's Egyptian army invaded. The intervention of Britain, France and Russia at Navarino in 1827 saved the revolution. Ioannis Kapodistrias, elected governor, arrived in 1828 and built a central administration at Nauplia, founding schools and a currency, the phoenix.
first-hellenic-republic.e: The London Protocol of 1830 recognised Greek independence. Kapodistrias was assassinated at Nauplia in October 1831, and chaos followed. In 1832 the great powers chose Otto of Bavaria as king, creating the Kingdom of Greece.

free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar.t: Small Hessian imperial city that became home to the Empire's supreme court in 1689, where the young Goethe trained and found the story of Werther.
free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar.o: Wetzlar grew around a collegiate church on the Lahn and received town privileges from Frederick Barbarossa, being treated as an imperial city from about 1180. It lay where trade roads crossed the river, and its cloth and leather trade made it prosperous in the 13th century, when work began on the large collegiate church known as the cathedral.
free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar.r: A council under the emperor's protection governed the town, but heavy debts and feuds in the 14th century left it weak, and it relied on neighbouring Hesse and Nassau. Its fortunes revived when the Imperial Chamber Court, the Reichskammergericht, moved there from Speyer in 1689 and stayed until 1806. Lawyers flocked to the town; Goethe worked at the court in 1772, and his stay inspired The Sorrows of Young Werther.
free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar.e: In 1803 Wetzlar lost its freedom and was given to Karl Theodor von Dalberg as a county. The Congress of Vienna assigned it to the Kingdom of Prussia in 1815. It is now a town in Hesse known for optics and the Leica camera.

free-imperial-city-of-rothenburg.t: Franconian imperial city above the Tauber whose medieval walls and streets survived almost intact, made famous by the legend of the Master Draught.
free-imperial-city-of-rothenburg.o: Rothenburg grew below a Hohenstaufen castle on a spur above the Tauber valley in the 12th century. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen, King Rudolf I confirmed its status as an imperial city in 1274, and it soon threw off the last rights of outside lords.
free-imperial-city-of-rothenburg.r: A patrician council ruled. Under the mayor Heinrich Toppler, who died in prison in 1408 after a conflict with King Wenceslaus, the city built up one of the largest rural territories of any imperial city. It lived from farming, cattle and wool. Rothenburg adopted the Reformation in 1544. In 1631 it was taken by Tilly's imperial army, an episode remembered in the legend of the Master Draught.
free-imperial-city-of-rothenburg.e: Impoverished by war, the city stagnated, which preserved its medieval appearance. It lost its freedom to Bavaria in 1802 to 1803 and became a celebrated tourist destination; its old town was carefully restored after damage in 1945.

free-imperial-city-of-isny.t: An Allgäu linen town that bought its freedom in 1365 and turned Protestant while its abbey stayed Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-isny.o: Isny grew around a Benedictine abbey founded in 1096 by the counts of Veringen-Altshausen. The market beside the abbey became a town in the 13th century and passed to the Truchsesses of Waldburg, from whom it bought its freedom in 1365, becoming a free imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-isny.r: Isny's prosperity came from linen weaving and trade with Italy. The town adopted the Reformation in the 16th century; around 1540 the reformer Paul Fagius ran a Hebrew printing press there with the scholar Elijah Levita. The Benedictine abbey, which gained its own imperial status in 1781, remained a Catholic enclave.
free-imperial-city-of-isny.e: In 1803 the town and abbey were given to the counts of Quadt as compensation for lost lands, and in 1806 they passed to the Kingdom of Württemberg. Isny im Allgäu keeps much of its wall and towers.

french-cilicia.t: The French military occupation of Cilicia after the First World War, whose collapse ended the hopes of returning Armenian refugees.
french-cilicia.o: Under the Armistice of Mudros, British and then French forces occupied Cilicia from late 1918, and in 1919 France took over full responsibility, administering it as part of the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration. Tens of thousands of Armenian survivors of the deportations returned with French support.
french-cilicia.r: France governed through military administrators such as Colonel Edouard Bremond, relying partly on the Armenian Legion. The administration encouraged Armenian resettlement in Adana, Marash and Aintab, which alarmed Turkish Muslims. Nationalist resistance grew, and in January-February 1920 fighting in Marash ended with a French withdrawal and the deaths of thousands of Armenians. Sieges followed at Urfa and Aintab.
french-cilicia.e: By the Treaty of Ankara in October 1921 France recognised the nationalist Government of the Grand National Assembly and withdrew from Cilicia by early 1922. Most Armenians left with the French, many settling in Syria and Lebanon.

free-imperial-city-of-colmar.t: Alsatian wine town that was an imperial city and member of the Decapolis league until Louis XIV's France absorbed it in the 1670s.
free-imperial-city-of-colmar.o: Colmar grew from a Carolingian estate on the Lauch in Upper Alsace. The Hohenstaufen favoured it, and it received town rights in 1226 from Frederick II, becoming an imperial city. In 1354 it joined the Decapolis, the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities under the imperial bailiff at Haguenau.
free-imperial-city-of-colmar.r: Guilds and patricians shared power in the council. Colmar prospered from the Alsatian wine trade and crafts, and the painter Martin Schongauer worked there in the 15th century. The city adopted the Reformation in 1575. During the Thirty Years War it was held by Swedish and then French troops, and the Decapolis came under French protection.
free-imperial-city-of-colmar.e: French forces occupied Colmar in 1673, and the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679 confirmed French rule. It was German from 1871 to 1918 and again from 1940 to 1945, and is now a French town famous for its old quarter and the Isenheim Altarpiece.

free-territory.t: Nestor Makhno's anarchist zone in south-eastern Ukraine, run by peasant councils and defended by a revolutionary army in the Civil War.
free-territory.o: Nestor Makhno, an anarchist from Huliaipole, organised peasant partisans against the Austro-German occupiers and the Ukrainian State in 1918. As the Revolutionary Insurgent Army of Ukraine grew, it controlled a large area between the Dnieper and the Sea of Azov, which anarchists called the Free Territory.
free-territory.r: The movement rejected any state, organising regional congresses of peasants, workers and insurgents, free soviets and communes, while anarchist thinkers such as Volin ran its cultural work. In practice it was a military zone held by Makhno's highly mobile cavalry and machine-gun carts. The insurgents fought Germans, nationalists and Bolsheviks, and in September 1919 their victory at Peregonovka disrupted Denikin's march on Moscow.
free-territory.e: In 1920 Makhno allied with the Red Army against Wrangel, but once the Whites were beaten the Bolsheviks turned on the insurgents in November. After months of fighting Makhno escaped to Romania in August 1921 and died in Paris in 1934.

federal-state-of-austria.t: Authoritarian Catholic corporate state in Austria between 1934 and the German annexation of 1938.
federal-state-of-austria.o: Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss suspended parliament in March 1933 and ruled by decree, banning the Communists and Austrian Nazis. After crushing the Social Democrats in the civil war of February 1934, he proclaimed a new constitution on 1 May 1934, creating the Federal State of Austria based on Catholic corporatist ideas.
federal-state-of-austria.r: The regime ruled through a single party, the Fatherland Front, and corporate bodies in place of a parliament, drawing on the papal encyclical Quadragesimo Anno and on Mussolini's support. Dollfuss was murdered by Austrian Nazis in a failed putsch in July 1934. His successor Kurt Schuschnigg tried to preserve independence while yielding to German pressure under the 1936 July Agreement.
federal-state-of-austria.e: In March 1938 Schuschnigg called a referendum on independence, but under German threats he resigned. German troops entered Austria on 12 March 1938, and the country was annexed to Nazi Germany in the Anschluss.

free-imperial-city-of-nordhausen.t: Thuringian imperial city at the foot of the Harz, an early adopter of the Reformation and long famous for its grain spirits.
free-imperial-city-of-nordhausen.o: Nordhausen grew around a royal palace and a convent founded by Queen Matilda in the 10th century. In 1220 Emperor Frederick II freed it from the convent's lordship, making it an imperial city. It allied with Erfurt and Mühlhausen in a Thuringian city league and traded within the Hanseatic network.
free-imperial-city-of-nordhausen.r: Patricians held power until a guild uprising in 1375 brought craftsmen onto the council. The city was surrounded by the lands of the counts of Hohnstein and Stolberg and relied on imperial protection and alliances. Nordhausen adopted Lutheranism very early, in the 1520s. Brewing and later grain spirits, the Nordhäuser Korn, were its best-known products.
free-imperial-city-of-nordhausen.e: The city lost its freedom in 1802 to Prussia, belonged to the Kingdom of Westphalia from 1807 to 1813, and then returned to Prussia. It was heavily bombed in 1945, and it is now a town in Thuringia.

free-imperial-city-of-weissenburg.t: A small Franconian imperial city on the old Roman frontier that governed itself as a free city until 1802.
free-imperial-city-of-weissenburg.o: Weissenburg lies beside the Roman fort of Biriciana on the Raetian limes. A Carolingian royal estate stood there, and Charlemagne's attempted canal between the Rhine and Danube basins, the Fossa Carolina, lay nearby. The town was a royal possession of the Hohenstaufen and by the end of the 13th century counted as a free imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-weissenburg.r: A council of burghers governed the town and its small territory. Its economy rested on crafts, traffic on the road from Nuremberg to Augsburg and the stone quarries of the Franconian Jura. The city adopted the Lutheran Reformation and belonged to the Franconian Circle. Above it stood the Wülzburg fortress, held by the margraves of the Principality of Brandenburg-Ansbach, its constant rivals.
free-imperial-city-of-weissenburg.e: Weissenburg was occupied by Bavaria in 1802 and formally annexed in 1803 under the mediatisation of the imperial cities. It is now Weißenburg in Bayern, known for its Roman baths and a hoard of Roman treasure found there in 1979.

free-imperial-city-of-memmingen.t: Swabian imperial city where the Twelve Articles of the German Peasants' War were drawn up in 1525, often called the first charter of human rights in Europe.
free-imperial-city-of-memmingen.o: Memmingen grew as a Guelph market town at the meeting of trade routes between the Allgäu and the Danube, passing to the Hohenstaufen. After their fall, King Rudolf I recognised it as an imperial city in 1286, granting it the law of Überlingen.
free-imperial-city-of-memmingen.r: Guilds shared power with patricians on the council. Linen and the salt trade brought wealth. In 1525 representatives of the rebellious peasants met in Memmingen and adopted the Twelve Articles, drafted by Sebastian Lotzer and the preacher Christoph Schappeler. In 1530 the city joined the Tetrapolitan Confession and later adopted Lutheranism. Wallenstein had his headquarters there in 1630.
free-imperial-city-of-memmingen.e: Memmingen lost its freedom in 1802 when Bavaria annexed it. It is now a town in Bavaria, which commemorates the Twelve Articles and the peasants' parliament of 1525 in its old guild hall.

free-state-of-oldenburg.t: North-west German republic that succeeded the grand duchy and in 1932 elected one of the first Nazi state governments.
free-state-of-oldenburg.o: Grand Duke Frederick Augustus II abdicated in November 1918, and Oldenburg became a free state, with a constitution adopted in 1919. It kept the detached principalities of Lübeck around Eutin and Birkenfeld in the Hunsrück.
free-state-of-oldenburg.r: Oldenburg was rural, with dairy farming in the marshes and moors and a naval port at Wilhelmshaven nearby. Its Lutheran north and Catholic south around Cloppenburg and Vechta differed politically. In 1932 the Nazis won an absolute majority, and Carl Röver formed one of the first Nazi state governments. In 1937 the Greater Hamburg Act transferred Lübeck and Birkenfeld to Prussia and gave Wilhelmshaven to Oldenburg.
free-state-of-oldenburg.e: Under the Nazis, Röver became Reich governor for Oldenburg and Bremen. After 1945 the state lay in the British zone, and in November 1946 it was merged with Hanover, Brunswick and Schaumburg-Lippe into the state of Lower Saxony. Oldenburg survives as a historic region and administrative name.

first-republic-of-venezuela.t: The first Spanish American colony to declare full independence, a federal republic that collapsed within a year amid earthquake and civil war.
first-republic-of-venezuela.o: After the Caracas junta of 19 April 1810 removed the captain-general of the Captaincy General of Venezuela, a congress met in 1811. Urged on by Francisco de Miranda and the young Simón Bolívar of the Patriotic Society, it declared independence on 5 July 1811, the first such declaration in Spanish America.
first-republic-of-venezuela.r: A federal constitution was adopted in December 1811, with an executive triumvirate including Cristóbal Mendoza. The republic abolished titles and the slave trade, but kept slavery and property qualifications for voting. Provinces such as Coro, Maracaibo and Guayana stayed royalist. On 26 March 1812 an earthquake destroyed Caracas and other patriot towns, and clergy presented it as divine punishment.
first-republic-of-venezuela.e: The royalist commander Domingo de Monteverde advanced on Caracas. Miranda, named dictator, capitulated at San Mateo in July 1812. He was handed to the Spanish by fellow officers, Bolívar among them, and died in a Cádiz prison in 1816.

free-imperial-city-of-munster.t: Small Alsatian imperial city in the Vosges valley of Saint Gregory, grown around an old abbey and remembered today for its cheese.
free-imperial-city-of-munster.o: Munster grew around the Benedictine abbey of Saint Gregory, founded in the 7th century in a Vosges valley west of Colmar. The town that formed beside the monastery won its freedom from the abbots and was recognised as an imperial city by Rudolf I in 1287. It later joined the Decapolis, the league of Alsatian imperial cities.
free-imperial-city-of-munster.r: The town shared authority over the valley with the abbey in a long and often bitter relationship. Its people lived from dairy farming, cheese, textiles and the valley's trade. The town and much of the valley adopted the Lutheran Reformation in the 1530s, while the abbey remained Catholic. Munster suffered heavily in the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-munster.e: French troops occupied the Decapolis, and the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679 confirmed French sovereignty. Munster was almost completely destroyed in the fighting of 1914 to 1915. It is now a town in Alsace famed for Munster cheese.

first-bulgarian-empire.t: Medieval Bulgarian state founded by Asparuh's Bulgars, which adopted Christianity, nurtured Slavonic literature and rivalled Byzantium for three centuries.
first-bulgarian-empire.o: Bulgars under Khan Asparuh crossed the Danube around 680 and defeated a Byzantine army. In 681 Byzantium recognised the new state, which joined Bulgars with the Seven Slavic Tribes and the Severi. Pliska became the first capital.
first-bulgarian-empire.r: Early khans ruled with a Bulgar aristocracy; Krum killed the emperor Nikephoros I in 811 and took Serdica. Boris I accepted Christianity in 864, and the disciples of Cyril and Methodius developed Slavonic writing, including the Cyrillic alphabet, at Preslav and Ohrid. Under Simeon I (893–927), who took the title tsar, Bulgaria dominated the Balkans and Preslav became the capital.
first-bulgarian-empire.e: Russian and Byzantine invasions in 968–971 took the east. Samuel ruled the west from Ohrid, but Basil II destroyed his army at Kleidion in 1014, and by 1018 Bulgaria was annexed by Byzantium. The Second Bulgarian Empire revived it in 1185.

federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.t: Federation of Serbia and Montenegro formed in 1992 from the remains of Yugoslavia, dominated by Slobodan Milošević and marked by sanctions and war.
federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.o: As the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia broke apart, the two remaining republics, Serbia and Montenegro, adopted a new constitution on 27 April 1992 creating the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It claimed to be the continuation of the old state, a claim most other states and the United Nations rejected. The writer Dobrica Ćosić was its first president.
federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.r: Real power lay with Slobodan Milošević, president of Serbia and from 1997 of the federation. United Nations sanctions over the wars in Croatia and Bosnia brought hyperinflation in 1993 and economic collapse. After the Dayton Agreement of 1995 came conflict in Kosovo, NATO bombing in 1999 and Kosovo's placement under UN administration. Montenegro under Milo Đukanović increasingly went its own way.
federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.e: Milošević was overthrown in the protests of 5 October 2000 after losing the election to Vojislav Koštunica, and was later sent to The Hague. The EU-brokered Belgrade Agreement of 2002 replaced the federation with Serbia and Montenegro in February 2003.

first-austrian-republic.t: Inter-war Austrian democracy, a small state left by the Habsburg collapse that slid into civil war and dictatorship.
first-austrian-republic.o: The Republic of German-Austria was renamed the Republic of Austria in October 1919 after the Treaty of Saint-Germain forbade union with Germany. The federal constitution of 1920, drafted with the help of Hans Kelsen, created a federal parliamentary republic with nine states, including Vienna and, from 1921, Burgenland.
first-austrian-republic.r: The republic was polarised between the Christian Social Party, strong in the countryside, and the Social Democrats of Red Vienna, who built large council housing estates. Each side had armed militias. Chancellor Ignaz Seipel stabilised the currency with a League of Nations loan in 1922. The burning of the Palace of Justice in 1927 and the Depression deepened the crisis.
first-austrian-republic.e: In March 1933 Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss suspended parliament. After a brief civil war in February 1934 the Social Democrats were banned, and the May 1934 constitution created the authoritarian Federal State of Austria.

free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg.t: Elbe port that grew from a Carolingian fort into the Hanseatic League's second city and remains an independent city-state of Germany today.
free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg.o: Hamburg began as a Carolingian fort and mission base and was refounded as a merchant settlement in the 12th century. Its port privileges are traditionally dated to a charter of Frederick Barbarossa of 1189, actually a later forgery but still celebrated as the port's birthday. An alliance with Lübeck in 1241 laid foundations for the Hanseatic League.
free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg.r: Merchant families ruled through the council and the mayors, with citizens represented after the Reformation. Hamburg became Lutheran in 1529 under Johannes Bugenhagen's church order. Brewing, the Elbe trade and later Atlantic commerce made it rich, and the Bank of Hamburg was founded in 1619. Its imperial immediacy was confirmed in 1618, and Denmark accepted it in 1768.
free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg.e: Napoleonic France annexed Hamburg in 1810 to 1814. It then joined the German Confederation and German Empire as a city-state, survived the Great Fire of 1842, and gained Altona and other towns in 1937. It is now a federal state of Germany and the country's largest port.

free-imperial-city-of-constance.t: Lake Constance city that hosted the great Council of 1414 to 1418, which ended the Western Schism and burned Jan Hus, before Austria absorbed it in 1548.
free-imperial-city-of-constance.o: Constance was a Roman fort and from about 600 the seat of the largest diocese in Germany. Its citizens gradually freed themselves from the bishop's rule, and the Hohenstaufen emperors granted privileges, so that by the late 12th century it was treated as an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-constance.r: Merchants and guilds shared power in the council. The city's fine linen was sold across Europe, and it was a member of Swabian and Lake Constance city leagues. From 1414 to 1418 it hosted the Council of Constance, which elected Pope Martin V, ending the Western Schism, and burned Jan Hus. In the 1520s the city adopted the Reformation under Ambrosius Blarer, and the bishop moved to Meersburg.
free-imperial-city-of-constance.e: As a member of the defeated Schmalkaldic League, Constance was taken by Charles V in 1548 and given to the Austrian Habsburgs, losing its freedom and returning to Catholicism. It stayed in Further Austria until passing to Baden in 1806.

federal-league.t: A league of provinces led by José Artigas that challenged Buenos Aires with a vision of federal democracy in the River Plate region.
federal-league.o: In 1814 José Gervasio Artigas, leader of the Eastern Province, drew the provinces of Entre Ríos, Corrientes, Santa Fe and Misiones, and briefly Córdoba, into an alliance against the centralism of Buenos Aires. Artigas took the title Protector of the Free Peoples. In 1815 the Congress of Oriente met at Concepción del Uruguay.
federal-league.r: The league was a loose alliance of provincial caudillos rather than a state. It defended provincial autonomy, free trade on the rivers and the rights of rural people. Artigas directed it from his camp at Purificación, near Paysandú on the Uruguay river. Indigenous Guaraní of the missions, led by Andrés Guazurary, fought with him.
federal-league.e: Portugal's invasion of the Banda Oriental from 1816 drained the league. After Artigas's defeat at Tacuarembó in 1820, his allies Francisco Ramírez and Estanislao López made peace with Buenos Aires in the Treaty of Pilar. Artigas went into exile in Paraguay, where he died in 1850.
