frentani.t: Oscan-speaking people of the central Adriatic coast, related to the Samnites, who became allies of Rome in 304 BCE.
frentani.o: The Frentani occupied the coastal hills of modern Molise and southern Abruzzo between the Sangro and the Fortore rivers. Ancient writers considered them of Samnite stock, and they spoke Oscan. Their history before Rome is known only from scattered references.
frentani.r: Their main centres included Histonium (Vasto), Anxanum (Lanciano) and Larinum, which some writers treated as a separate people. They farmed, herded and traded along the coast. They usually kept apart from the Samnite League and its wars with Rome.
frentani.e: The Frentani made an alliance with Rome in 304 BCE, at the end of the Second Samnite War, and fought for Rome against Hannibal. They joined the Italian rebels in the Social War of 91–88 BCE, then received citizenship and were absorbed into Roman Italy.

free-imperial-city-of-weil-der-stadt.t: Small Catholic imperial city surrounded by Protestant Württemberg, best known as the birthplace of the astronomer Johannes Kepler.
free-imperial-city-of-weil-der-stadt.o: Weil grew on the Würm west of Stuttgart and belonged to the Hohenstaufen, whose estates in the area passed to the Empire on their fall. It was then treated as an imperial city, confirmed in the 1270s, around 1275, its name, Weil the City, distinguishing it from nearby villages.
free-imperial-city-of-weil-der-stadt.r: A council of burghers ruled this small town with its handful of villages. It lived from farming, crafts and markets. Surrounded entirely by the Duchy of Württemberg, it often quarrelled with its powerful neighbour and remained Catholic when Württemberg turned Protestant. The astronomer Johannes Kepler was born there in 1571. Much of the town was burned in 1648 near the end of the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-weil-der-stadt.e: Württemberg finally annexed the town in 1802, ending its long resistance to its neighbour. It is now a small town in Baden-Württemberg, with a Kepler museum in the house where the astronomer was born.

frisii.t: Germanic people of the North Sea coast who lived on artificial mounds and defied Rome by force and by diplomacy.
frisii.o: The Frisii lived on the coastal marshes of the northern Netherlands between the Rhine and the Ems. To survive floods they built terps, artificial dwelling mounds raised over generations. They became tributaries of Rome after the campaigns of Drusus in 12 BCE.
frisii.r: They paid tribute in ox hides. Roman sources describe no kings but war leaders and envoys; in 58 CE Verritus and Malorix travelled to Rome and boldly took seats among the senators at Pompey's Theatre, winning Nero's admiration.
frisii.e: In 28 CE they revolted against exactions, hanging tax collectors and defeating the Romans at the Baduhenna wood. Rome later abandoned control. In the 4th century rising seas left much of the coast nearly deserted, and the area was resettled, later forming the Frisian Kingdom.

free-imperial-city-of-goslar.t: Harz imperial city of the Salian emperors' palace and the Rammelsberg silver mine, whose wealth made it a leading Hanseatic town.
free-imperial-city-of-goslar.o: Silver was found in the Rammelsberg near Goslar in the 10th century, and the Salian emperors built an imperial palace there, where Henry III often resided. The town grew rich from mining and metal trade. After the decline of royal power it gradually took control of its own affairs and was a free imperial city by around 1290.
free-imperial-city-of-goslar.r: A council dominated by mine owners and merchants ruled. Silver, copper and lead from the Rammelsberg brought Goslar great wealth, and it joined the Hanseatic League. The city adopted the Reformation in 1528. In the Treaty of Riechenberg of 1552 it lost control of the mine and forests to Henry the Younger of the Principality of Wolfenbüttel, beginning a long decline.
free-imperial-city-of-goslar.e: Goslar lost its freedom in 1802 to Prussia, belonged to the Kingdom of Westphalia from 1807 and to the Kingdom of Hanover from 1816. Its old town and the Rammelsberg mine are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

free-imperial-city-of-bopfingen.t: One of the smallest imperial cities of the Empire, a Swabian market town at the foot of the Ipf, a celebrated Celtic hillfort.
free-imperial-city-of-bopfingen.o: Bopfingen lies beneath the Ipf, a hill crowned by a major Celtic princely seat of the 6th and 5th centuries BCE. The medieval town grew under the Hohenstaufen and appears among the imperial cities in the imperial tax list of 1241.
free-imperial-city-of-bopfingen.r: Bopfingen was a modest market town with a tiny territory, governed by a council of burghers and dependent on its larger neighbour Nördlingen and on the Swabian city leagues. Its economy rested on farming, crafts and the local market. It adopted the Reformation in the 16th century and suffered heavily in the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-bopfingen.e: Bopfingen lost its freedom in 1802, passing first to the Electorate of Bavaria and in 1810 to the Kingdom of Württemberg. It is now a small town in Baden-Württemberg, and the Ipf is a protected archaeological site.

free-state-of-coburg.t: Brief Franconian republic that, after a 1919 referendum, chose to join Bavaria rather than Thuringia.
free-state-of-coburg.o: Duke Charles Edward of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha abdicated in November 1918. Coburg and Gotha, legally separate since 1826, went their own ways: Gotha joined Thuringia, while Coburg became a free state of its own, with its parliament meeting in Coburg.
free-state-of-coburg.r: The free state existed only briefly and had few powers beyond managing the transition. Its main question was its future: too small to survive alone, it had to choose between the new Thuringian state and Bavaria. In a referendum on 30 November 1919, about 88 per cent of voters chose Bavaria, partly because of Coburg's Franconian ties and Bavaria's favourable terms.
free-state-of-coburg.e: Under a state treaty Coburg joined the Free State of Bavaria on 1 July 1920, keeping certain guarantees for its institutions. Coburg Day still marks the event.

free-imperial-city-of-kaufbeuren.t: Allgäu imperial city on the Wertach, a linen-weaving town shared by Catholics and Protestants after the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-kaufbeuren.o: Kaufbeuren grew around a royal court on the Wertach under the Guelphs and Hohenstaufen, on the road from Augsburg into the Alps. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen it was recognised as an imperial city by Rudolf I in 1286.
free-imperial-city-of-kaufbeuren.r: A council of patricians and guilds governed. Linen and fustian weaving were the main trades. The city adopted the Reformation, but after 1648 Catholics and Lutherans shared its offices under the parity rules of the Peace of Westphalia. The Franciscan nun Crescentia of Kaufbeuren, later canonised, lived there in the 18th century.
free-imperial-city-of-kaufbeuren.e: Kaufbeuren lost its freedom in 1802 to Bavaria. After the Second World War German refugees from Gablonz in Bohemia settled its suburb of Neugablonz, bringing their glass and jewellery industry. It remains a town in Bavaria.

fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: A line of Delta kings of largely Canaanite descent who ruled the eastern Nile Delta as the Middle Kingdom weakened.
fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: As the Thirteenth Dynasty lost its grip, around 1725 BCE a separate line of kings established itself in the eastern Delta, probably at Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a), where a large population of Levantine origin had settled. Manetho placed the dynasty at Xois in the western Delta, but most scholars now locate it at Avaris.
fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: Very little is known. The best-attested king, Nehesy, whose name means 'the Nubian', left monuments at Avaris and Tell el-Muqdam and honoured Seth as lord of Avaris. Scarabs with royal names suggest a series of short reigns. The dynasty controlled the Delta's trade with the Levant, and its population buried their dead in Canaanite fashion, with donkeys and bronze weapons.
fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: The kingdom seems to have been weakened by famine and plague, and around 1650 BCE it was replaced by the Hyksos rulers of the Fifteenth Dynasty of Egypt, who also made Avaris their capital.

free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.t: The guild-run republic on the Rhine where Gutenberg experimented with printing and Martin Bucer led the Reformation, before Louis XIV annexed it in 1681.
free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.o: The burghers of Strasbourg had long resented the rule of their bishops. In 1262 they defeated Bishop Walter of Geroldseck at the battle of Hausbergen and won self-government, and the city soon became a free city of the Holy Roman Empire, outside the Prince-Bishopric of Strasbourg.
free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.r: From 1332 the guilds shared power with the patricians in a council and magistracy. Strasbourg traded along the Rhine, finished its cathedral spire in 1439, and hosted Johannes Gutenberg's early work. It adopted the Reformation in the 1520s under Martin Bucer, while Jacob Sturm led its diplomacy and Johannes Sturm founded its Gymnasium. The first printed newspaper appeared there in 1605.
free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.e: In 1681, during peacetime, Louis XIV's troops surrounded Strasbourg and forced it to surrender. It kept its Lutheran churches and local institutions, but became part of the Kingdom of France, confirmed by the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697.

free-imperial-city-of-giengen.t: A small Swabian imperial city on the Brenz, later known worldwide as the home of the Steiff teddy bear.
free-imperial-city-of-giengen.o: Giengen grew on the river Brenz in eastern Swabia as a Hohenstaufen royal town. After a period in which it was pledged to the counts of Helfenstein, the townspeople secured their freedom, and by 1391 Giengen was recognised as a free imperial city answerable only to the emperor.
free-imperial-city-of-giengen.r: A council governed the small town and its few villages. Giengen lived from crafts, linen and the market for the surrounding farms, and it adopted the Lutheran Reformation in the 16th century. Its position near the Danube exposed it to war, and in 1634, during the Thirty Years' War, it was almost completely burned.
free-imperial-city-of-giengen.e: In 1802 Giengen was annexed by Württemberg, becoming part of the Kingdom of Württemberg in 1806. In 1880 Margarete Steiff founded her toy business there, and Giengen an der Brenz remains the home of the Steiff company.
